You are a clinical information extraction system. Read ONE outpatient consultation transcript (lines like "[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): text") and return ONE JSON object with the clinical information it contains, in the trained clinical-extraction format. Return only the JSON.

Rules
- Use only what is said. Never invent or infer. Leave out every field and section that has no information.
- Record who said it (doctor, patient, nurse, caregiver, family_member, clinical_staff, unknown), in lower case.
- A denied finding goes in negative_findings, never in symptoms. A doctor's question is not a fact: use the answer.
- A medicine the patient takes is not an allergy. A stopped medicine is not current. Dose, frequency, route and indication belong only to the medicine they were said for.
- Doctor impressions are provisional or differential, and only if the doctor stated one. Do not add a diagnosis the doctor declined to give.
- Use the right status for plan items (planned, completed, recommended, conditional). Do not add a follow-up that was not arranged.
- If speakers disagree or a detail is unclear (dose, date, allergy, name), keep both statements and describe the real doubt in clinical_uncertainties.
- Cite one or two segment ids per item in evidence_ids. clinical_evidence is []. All confidence fields are null.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on back, Mr. Hale. I'll get your numbers before Dr. Okonkwo steps in.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is one fifty-two over eighty-eight. Heart rate seventy-six. Oxygen sat ninety-seven percent. Respirations sixteen.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Dr. Okonkwo. You're here for what?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Checkup.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything bothering you?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Sixty-four.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): I asked about chest pain. Yes or no?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Alright. Cholesterol bloodwork, and I'll see you in a year. No heart tracing.
[SEG0013] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Wait. He pulls up on our stairs. Says his chest gets tight.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Not pulling up. Just slow.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tightness in the chest, yes or no?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Only on stairs?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Stairs. And fast walking.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pain?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Tight. Like a band.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does it go down the arm?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): The arm. Any pain there?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Jaw?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sweaty with it?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sick to your stomach?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0031] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He gets short of breath. I hear him from the kitchen.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0033] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Well, actually, he is winded every time. He won't say so.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long has the tightness been there?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks.
[SEG0036] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A month. Since the lake weekend. And the parking garage was a mess today, just saying.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): So somewhere between two weeks and a month. You don't agree, and I won't force it.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any tightness while you sit still?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): It quits if you rest?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): You on a blood pressure pill?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Lisinopril. Twenty. Mornings.
[SEG0045] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The bottle says ten milligrams. One each morning. I line them up.
[SEG0046] person_1 (NURSE): Chart from his last visit says lisinopril twenty milligrams daily.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): We can't sort that dose here. Aspirin?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Eighty-one milligrams?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Every day?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0053] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He skips a lot of days. My metformin is for my diabetes, that's mine, not his. His sister mailed him biotin for her hair and he never opened it.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any drug allergies?
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0056] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Penicillin. His face swelled years ago. He always denies it.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0058] person_3 (DOCTOR): Past surgeries?
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0060] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Quit.
[SEG0062] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ten years ago. He retired from the post office last spring.
[SEG0063] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any alcohol?
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0065] person_3 (DOCTOR): Lungs are clear. Heart is regular, no murmur. Chest wall isn't tender.
[SEG0066] person_3 (DOCTOR): This could be angina, though I'm not calling it for sure. Forget the cholesterol-only visit in a year. I almost ordered a stress test, but I won't. ECG today, plus bloods: CBC, a metabolic panel, lipids, and a troponin.
[SEG0067] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come back in one week. If the tightness starts while you're resting, or you get sweaty or sick with it, go to the ER. Stay on the lisinopril each morning, take the aspirin every day instead of skipping, and ease off fast walking until we know.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right then, come on in. What do you need help with?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): mainly more breathless than usual there's a couple of other things, but that's the main one
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): what's the timeline, when did it begin?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Around three weeks... no wait, you know, it's more like about two weeks.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): can you describe it a bit more for me? How strong it is what the pattern is what helps
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): it happens once or twice a day about a three out of ten
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about more sputum, a bit yellow, have you noticed that?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, since last Tuesday.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): are you allergic to anything? Any allergies to medicines or foods?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): no allergies at all
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any regular medication tablets or creams?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): no, none
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): alright, do you have any medical conditions I should know about?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): no, I've always been fairly healthy
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any previous surgeries?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): what does a normal day of food look like?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Lots of rice, lentils and some fruit.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is there someone at home?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): My husband and I live above the shop.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): let me check a few things any coughing up blood swollen ankles or chest pain?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): nope nothing like that
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): okay is your urine normal no changes?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): that's normal as far as I know
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any muscle or joint problems besides this?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No, joints are fine.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): can I check a few measurements before we carry on?
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): nearly done with the readings..
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): okay: pulse is 103 beats a a minute, height 181 centimetres and oxygen saturation is 92 percent, BMI works out to 22.9, temp 36.9 degrees, respiratory rate 20, weight 75 kilos, blood pressure 130 over 87.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that that alright doctor?
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll interpret them after the the examination
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, over here please and I'll take a look.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): of course
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): hold that for a second
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): There is wheeze at both bases and your oxygen is a little low.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Please sit back down.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): so, to recap quickly you've had more breathless than usual for about two weeks, and no coughing up blood or chest pain
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): yes, you've got it
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): I want a chest X-ray done that's for COPD flare. What I'm giving you is prednisolone 30 milligrams once a day five days. That should help with COPD flare. Use your inhaler regularly and get seen if you are not better in three days. See me again in one week
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that's manageable.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): right that's the plan do you wanna ask me anything?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright, thanks, take care.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): all the best

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Doctor, hi, where would you like me to put my coat?
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Of course, leave it there. How can I help?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): So the thing is, I've got pelvic pain.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): What's the timeline, when did it begin?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): About... well, about a week.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How frequently does it come?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Honestly, on and off.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other symptoms with it?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): It usually comes with a smelly discharge.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had pelvic pain before, or is this the first time?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, so I had a similar thing a couple of years ago. It went away.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's run through your medicines.
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Tiotropium inhaler. I take it once a day. Erm, I'm supposed to take it regularly, but I don't always manage. Aspirin I don't take anymore.

[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No, um, that side's been fine.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you active?

[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, do you follow any particular diet?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Fever was there, the clinic doctor gave an antibiotic. Fever settled. The cough did not go, still every morning, with white sticky phlegm.

[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Say the number again please. The cursor moved out of the box. How many cigarettes in a day?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly twenty. If I am busy in the shop, sometimes less. Count it as twenty, don't make me repeat.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any diabetes or blood pressure? The problem list on this screen looks mixed up.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): That metformin is my wife's. She has sugar, she takes metformin five hundred morning and night. I don't have sugar. Last time they told me my pressure is normal.

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Beclomethasone. Two hundred. Two puffs morning and night is what is written. I am not doing it like that, I already said.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the antibiotic for that infection, are you still taking it?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Amoxicillin. Five days, three times a day. The course is finished, I stopped last week. No tablets now.

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): It feels tight inside, yes. Can we finish soon, I want to go and lie down.

[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): No oxygen today. Smoking is the part we can still change. I am offering you quitting support with the cessation clinic. They can start nicotine replacement if you are willing.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I will think. Cold turkey I cannot do. Don't lecture me, I already know twenty is too much, and I am irritable enough.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): I will refer you to that clinic. Please also use the beclomethasone every day, two puffs in the morning and two at night, not only when you remember. Salbutamol when you are breathless, maximum four times in a day.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Every day the brown one, fine, I will try. My sister keeps biotin and she said take the same for hair fall. I told her nonsense, that bottle is hers.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Leave the biotin, it is not your medicine and it will not help the lungs. If the breathlessness suddenly gets worse, or the fever comes back, or you see blood, don't wait, come back.

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can ease if the smoking reduces and the inhaler is taken daily, but not in two days. I want to see you in four weeks. If you are worse before that, come earlier, don't sit at home.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks is okay. Last time somebody talked of a chest x-ray and nothing happened. Are you actually doing it, or only talking.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): I will book the chest x-ray, so we are not missing anything else after that infection. Ask at the desk on the way out, they will have the form.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Good. Is there more? I am exhausted, that corridor was too much.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): That is all. Inhalers as I said, the quitting referral, the x-ray, and a review in four weeks. Any questions?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Just make the morning cough less. That is the only thing I want.

[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How many days or weeks has it been?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): About... well, five days.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How strong would you say it is?

[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How frequently does it come?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): It's, It's all the time.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had a sore throat earlier?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, about the same, two months. And slight aching, too. With slight aching, it comes and goes.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about your medical history?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): I have anxiety.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): I follow. Yes, anxiety is known to us, good to have that clear.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): What do you take on a normal day?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): It's escitalopram, 10 milligrams, once a day. Honey and lemon, at night.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Before we go further, any allergies?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Grass pollen. I come out in... well, itchy eyes.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): How are your meals?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): I grab fast food at lunch most days.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, do you do any exercise?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): I swim twice a week.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had fever, by any chance?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no fever.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any breathlessness, chest pain or coughing up blood at all?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): No breathlessness, chest pain or coughing up blood, none of it.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you noticed any weakness, or anything odd with your balance?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): No, that's all normal.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about your tummy and bowels, anything unusual there?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, no, all normal there.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me quickly check your readings.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's it, just a little longer...
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay: respiratory rate 14, pulse 73. And saturation 98 percent, pressure 124 over 71.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look at the area, I'll be gentle.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Right.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stay as you are for a moment.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your chest is clear and your oxygen is normal.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): You can sit up now. Having listened and examined, this is probably acute viral bronchitis.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): What are the odds it's serious?
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): I understand the worry. At the moment I'd say it's acute viral bronchitis, and we'll watch how it goes. I'd like you back if not better in three weeks.

[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): See you soon.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mrs Botha, in you come. Have a seat. What's the problem today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, doctor, the parking was hectic, we sat at that robot by the mall for ages, and Thandi wouldn't let me get out. But ja, it's the burning again when I pass urine.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Burning when you pass urine. How many times this year?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): This is the third time this year. Um, well, actually, maybe the fourth, if I count February. That one went away quick.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): This bout. How many days?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Three days. It started Wednesday. Or, hang on, Wednesday was Pick n Pay. Ja, three days, I'm pretty sure.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Doctor, she told me on Sunday already. That's five days, not three.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Sunday was the braai, Thandi. My eyes were stinging from the smoke, that's all. The urine burning is three days. I think.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): So roughly three to six days. I won't nail it further. Any blood in the urine?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No blood that I've seen.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Passing urine more often than usual?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): All the time, hey. I was squirming in the car.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): At night?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Two times. No, two or three times a night. I was up again.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I counted four times last night. The passage light woke me each time.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok, four then. I lose track when I'm half asleep.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Thandi put the thermometer on me yesterday and it was normal.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pain in the back, or in the side over the kidney?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Back's fine. I can still bend to the oven.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any vaginal discharge, itching, or a bad smell?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. Definitely not.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Taken anything for it?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, shame, I shouldn't have, my sister Liesl left amoxicillin, those two-fifty ones, from her tooth. No, wait, I'm mixing it up, it was ciprofloxacin, five hundred milligrams I think, twice a day for this burning.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): For how many days?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Three days. Ag, no, two days. I finished them on Tuesday, swallowed the last one with my tea.
[SEG0027] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She skipped the evening tablet, doctor. Both nights. I put it in the dish and it was still there in the morning.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I forgot once. Well, actually, maybe both nights. Don't look at me like that, my head's full.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): What do you take regularly?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): A little white pill for my blood pressure, I can never remember the silly name. And simvastatin for the cholesterol, ten milligrams... no, twenty milligrams, at night.
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That white tablet, the label's rubbed off. I thought it was perindopril, then I thought amlodipine. I really couldn't say.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. The blood pressure and the cholesterol. How long on the pressure one?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Since my sixties. I'm seventy-one now, so years and years. Thandi lives in with me, she tries to keep the pills straight.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the simvastatin, how long?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Five years? Ja, about five years. My late husband was on the same one, funny enough.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Speaking of him, he lived for the cricket. Did you see the Proteas on Saturday? I nearly fell off the couch.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): I didn't watch it.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No, man, just quickly. That catch at midwicket. Thandi was shouting at the television.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I was shouting because of the volume, not the cricket. I don't follow it.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): You do so. You asked me who was bowling. And my grandson Liam, he's nine, he bowls in the yard with a tennis ball and knocks the pot plants over.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mrs Botha, we should...
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): And then Eskom cut us in the middle of the over. Load shedding, stage four, right when they needed a boundary. Candles out like it's nineteen eighty.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The candles are in the sideboard. We were fine.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, and the neighbour's Jack Russell went mad in the dark. Yaps at the gate every time a bakkie goes past.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): I need to finish.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry, sorry. The drive home will be just as bad, school traffic and all. Liam's concert is on Thursday, he's a tree, a paper tree.
[SEG0047] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We'll talk about the concert later, Maggie.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): The weather's been lovely for it, though. Not too hot, a breeze off the mountain. I told him he'll wilt if he stands in the sun in that costume.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Back to you, please.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. I ramble when I'm nervous. It's embarrassing, this whole visit.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, about what you asked, down below, I didn't want to say it. There is a bit of itching on the outside, not discharge. And I don't have a smell, that part was true.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Itching on the outside only. The burning is still when the urine comes?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. The burning is when the urine comes, and the itch is on the skin, separate. It's mild, more annoying than sore.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you sexually active?
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'm a widow. Not for years. Nothing like that.
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to stamp one label on this yet. It may be another bladder infection, possibly the fourth this year, or it may be irritation on the vaginal side, the itch. I am not calling it a sexually transmitted infection, and I won't decide until we see what the urine shows.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it dangerous? My neighbour had a kidney business and she was in hospital a week, on a drip, the whole story. I don't want that.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): I can't say that from this chat. I'm sending a midstream urine for microscopy and culture. The lab sister at the hatch will give you the pot.
[SEG0059] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Must I go in with her for the sample?
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): If she wants you there, yes. And nobody takes another antibiotic out of a relative's cupboard.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): I won't. Liesl's pills are finished anyway. I felt silly even starting them.
[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): Drink plenty of water today and tomorrow.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): Water, ja. Not my rooibos? I live on rooibos, six cups, easy.
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): Water is what I want. Rooibos won't harm you, but it doesn't count as the water.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok. And if this carries on?
[SEG0066] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back if you're still burning in three days. Sooner if you get a fever or pain in the back, though you haven't got those now.
[SEG0067] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll bring her back if it isn't settling. I've got the car most mornings.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): Mornings Thandi does Checkers. We always get the rotisserie chicken, and if Liam is with us he eats half before we're home.
[SEG0069] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's between you and Liam. Do the urine before you leave. The form goes to reception.
[SEG0070] person_2 (PATIENT): Reception, ja. The lady with the red glasses was sharp about my medical aid last month. I nearly wrote a letter to the manager.
[SEG0071] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not my department. Questions about what I've said?
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): The cipro. Did I mess the test up by taking it already?
[SEG0073] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can muddy the culture. We still send the urine. I'm not starting another antibiotic today.
[SEG0074] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Thank you, doctor. We'll do the bottle on the way out.
[SEG0075] person_2 (PATIENT): If the Proteas win tonight and I miss it, I'm blaming this queue. Only joking. Thanks, hey.
[SEG0076] person_1 (DOCTOR): On you go. Reception has the form.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, Mr Hale. The slip from the desk just says back, so start wherever you like. Is this your wife with you?
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sandra. I booked him in, or he'd still be at work pretending he's fine.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Back.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Low back, or higher?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Low.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Left, right, or both?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Left.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long now?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Three.
[SEG0010] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's rounding it down. We moved house eight weeks ago, and it started that weekend, shifting wardrobes and boxes.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): What sort of work is it you do?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): Warehouse.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heavy lifting in the warehouse, and that flares the pain?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Score it out of ten.
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): Seven.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Constant, or on and off?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Constant.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything take the edge off?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Lying.
[SEG0021] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sofa every night. The dog's furious about the missed walks, and that animal thinks it runs the house.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the dog out of the notes.
[SEG0023] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He'll be glad someone said it. Right, back to the back.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me say the pain back to you. Left-sided low back pain, constant, seven out of ten, worse with lifting, eased by lying down. On timing you said three weeks and Sandra said eight, since the move, so I'll call it approximately three to eight weeks, not a precise date.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it travel into a leg?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Leg.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): The leg pain, which leg, and how far down does it go?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Left calf.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Painkillers. What have you actually taken?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): What strength are the tablets?
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): Two hundred.
[SEG0034] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. He buys four hundred milligram ibuprofen and takes two of them when it's bad.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): So for the ibuprofen I can't tell whether a dose is two hundred or eight hundred milligrams. I won't record a dose.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you taking them three times a day, as the packet usually says?
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0038] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He isn't taking them three times a day. He forgets, then he has a handful at bedtime.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): So whether he takes them as directed is anyone's guess. Any other regular medicines?
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Blood pressure.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you know its name?
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): White one.
[SEG0043] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Little white blood pressure tablet, every morning, for years. I almost called it amlodipine and that's me guessing, so scrub that.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Unnamed blood pressure tablet it is. You've got high blood pressure, yes?
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or tingling in the legs or feet?
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Problems with the waterworks at all?
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): Parking.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not the car park. Passing urine. Hesitancy, leaking, anything like that?
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight down without trying?
[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are your clothes looser?
[SEG0055] person_3 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll treat that as not a proper yes. No weight loss recorded. Fevers, or drenching sweats?
[SEG0057] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bowel accidents, or numbness around the saddle, the groin and back passage?
[SEG0059] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any drug allergies?
[SEG0061] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): On the couch, please. Looking at you, lumbar flexion is limited, and you're tender in the left lower lumbar muscles.
[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): Straight leg raise on the left reproduces the calf pain at about fifty degrees. Power at the ankle and big toe is normal, no foot drop, and light touch on the foot is intact.
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking mechanical low back pain, nothing alarming in the answers so far. Plan A, then: no scan, stay on the ibuprofen, I refer you to physio now, and I see you in six weeks.
[SEG0065] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hang on. The toes. Tell the doctor what the van does.
[SEG0066] person_3 (PATIENT): Tingle.
[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): You said no numbness a minute ago. Which toes, and is it tingling?
[SEG0068] person_3 (PATIENT): Left. Sometimes.
[SEG0069] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Left toes go tingly in the van. And the pain wakes him most nights. He's been up at two again.
[SEG0070] person_3 (PATIENT): Wakes.
[SEG0071] person_1 (DOCTOR): That new bit changes my mind. Scrap the immediate physio and the six-week review. The toe symptoms push this past a simple strain.
[SEG0072] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stop the ibuprofen. Start paracetamol, one gram by mouth, four times a day, for the back pain. I did wonder about naproxen five hundred milligrams twice a day and I'm not doing that, not with the blood pressure tablet and an anti-inflammatory already.
[SEG0073] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll arrange an MRI of the lumbar spine because of the left calf pain and the tingling toes. My working impression is mechanical low back pain with possible left nerve root irritation. A disc prolapse is on the differential, not a diagnosis I'll stamp today.
[SEG0074] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the scan is clear, we might refer you to physio afterwards. Keep moving gently, no heavy warehouse lifting until the scan is back, and if you cannot pass urine, develop saddle numbness, or a leg gives way, go to A&E the same day.
[SEG0075] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in two weeks.
[SEG0076] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We will.
[SEG0077] person_3 (PATIENT): Ta.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. Your daughter's brought you in about these turns. Dizzy, is that right?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, yes, a bit, when I stand up. But I haven't fallen, doctor, I just sort of slid. I'm worried it's something awful. Is it a stroke?
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Mum, you went down twice. Once by the kettle and once getting off the loo. I had to lift you. That's not sliding.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It wasn't a proper fall though. My legs just went a bit soft. I didn't black out or anything.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Twice. When?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, the first was... I think Thursday? Or was it the week before. I can't pin it down. Sorry.
[SEG0007] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thursday last week, and the Monday before that. So just under a fortnight.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dizzy only on standing?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, I get up from the settee and the room goes swimmy, and it frightens me. Sitting I'm alright. How long does that sort of thing last, normally?
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Seconds or minutes?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): A few seconds, then it eases if I hold the chair. Sometimes a minute. I don't know exactly.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no pain. Should I be worried about my heart though? My neighbour had a heart attack and she was dizzy.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): No shortness of breath?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No, breathing's fine. I am tired though, ever so washed out this last fortnight.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Headache? Weakness in one arm?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No headache, and my arms are alright, both of them. Why, do you think it's a stroke? Please just tell me.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not from what you've said. Tablets. Blood pressure and a sleeping tablet, yes?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, amlodipine, that's ten milligrams in the morning, and the other blood pressure one, ramipril, and zopiclone at night. I do take them. Do I have to stop them all? I won't sleep.
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ramipril is five milligrams. Zopiclone is seven point five. She takes the zopiclone every night, doctor, has done for years. The amlodipine she sometimes misses if she's rushing.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't miss them. Well, maybe once or twice. Not really.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): So amlodipine ten milligrams most mornings, ramipril five, zopiclone seven point five at night. Any allergies?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing I'm allergic to. Is the zopiclone the problem? I read they make old people fall.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Possibly. I'll stop the zopiclone and leave the blood pressure tablets as they are.
[SEG0025] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's been on that sleeping tablet since Dad died, about five-ish years. If you stop it she'll be up all night. The dizziness is in the morning, after she's stood up, not in the night.
[SEG0026] person_4 (NURSE): Sorry to butt in. Lying blood pressure a hundred and fifty-two over eighty-six, pulse seventy-four. Standing, after a minute, a hundred and ten over sixty-eight, pulse ninety-six.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. That drop changes things. Forget stopping the zopiclone. We'll stop the amlodipine instead and keep the ramipril and the sleeping tablet for now.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Stop the amlodipine completely? Not just a smaller dose? What if my blood pressure shoots up? And can I still take the zopiclone tonight?
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, stop amlodipine from today. Ramipril five milligrams stays. Zopiclone seven point five you can take tonight. We'll recheck the pressure.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Will I feel worse before I feel better? I'm really anxious about falling again, even if I say I only slid.
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She slid because her legs went. She was on the floor both times. I think you should know that properly.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Noted. No blackout, you said. Any palpitations?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No, it doesn't race. I just feel panicky sitting here, that's all. Is ninety-six too fast?
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): That pulse was on standing. It's acceptable. Drink plenty, stand up slowly, and sit if it swims. Don't drive until this settles.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't drive. Should I get a frame? And what about the chemist, do I just not collect the amlodipine?
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't collect it. No frame today. We'll sort a review on the way out.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): What if I go down again tomorrow? Do I ring you or nine nine nine? I need to know which.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you black out, injure yourself, or can't get up, it's nine nine nine. Otherwise ring the surgery the next morning.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll stay with her tonight. She lives alone usually, but I'm there till Sunday.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): You don't have to fuss. I'm fine, honestly, mostly. Will stopping one tablet really fix the swimming feeling?
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's the most likely culprit, given that standing drop. Not definite until we recheck. Any questions left that aren't repeats?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Just... if the ramipril is five milligrams, is that a lot? I get muddled with the numbers.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's a standard dose. Keep taking it. Reception will book you back in one week.

[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any time of day it's worse?

[SEG0012] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It is worse at night. I've heard him from the landing, even if he plays it down.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): When you cough, any blood? Any phlegm?

[SEG0017] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His trousers are sliding down. I've seen him hitch them up.
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Well, the clothes are looser, I'll give you that, belt's in a tighter hole. I wasn't trying to lose any. It's not a problem.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right now, any fever, any chest pain, any shortness of breath?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): No fever, no chest pain, not breathless. I walk the dog without stopping.

[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the plan is a chest X-ray. I want to see the lungs rather than guess. I'll request it today.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Bit much for a tickle, isn't it?
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's only a plain chest film, not a fuss. While we're here, what medicines are you taking?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Amlodipine, five milligrams, no, ten milligrams, once a day, for the blood pressure. I did try Covonia for a few nights and then I stopped, it did nothing.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): High blood pressure, then, ongoing, on the ten milligram dose. Any inhaler?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): No inhaler. The blood pressure has been years, it's fine, they keep an eye on it.
[SEG0032] person_1 (NURSE): I can send the chest X-ray request to the community list this afternoon, if that's the plan.

[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Alright, alright. Can we finish? The car park's daylight robbery.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nearly. If you start coughing blood, or you get properly short of breath, don't wait for that appointment, come back the same day or go to A&E.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, yeah, if that happens I'll come in. Are we done now?

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): We sat on the bridge forty minutes, and a guy in a pickup had the country station so loud the windows buzzed. Then a huge flock of geese went over, hundreds of them, heading south.

[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Did it? I had a runny nose for a few days back then and that cleared up. The cough stuck around.

[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Right, ramipril, for the blood pressure. Yeah. I don't know, the cough seemed to turn up around then. Could still be the cold, I reckon.

[SEG0023] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's pretty good with it. I see him take it at breakfast.
[SEG0024] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Speaking of that drive to Geelong, it was a shocker. The ring road was absolutely choked.

[SEG0027] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Until that collapse after tea. I nearly turned it off.

[SEG0052] person_1 (NURSE): Did you want me to print a path form, or are we leaving bloods?

[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): What happens, exactly?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, a tight feeling, like squeezing, in the centre of the chest. Climbing stairs brings it, walking fast also, and stairs are worse. If I slow down or I stop, it fades in a minute or two. Well, actually, I would not call it pain.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Only on exertion, not while sitting?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Not while sitting. Only when I push myself. I am tired of saying it.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Since when?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Since Diwali or after. I cannot date it properly. Maybe it started before that also, I really don't know.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any sweating when it comes?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No sweating.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it spread to the arm or the jaw?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It stays in the chest only. And honestly I am fed up. Half an hour for parking, what a waste.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which blood pressure tablet do you take?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlong. For the high BP.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dose, and how many times a day?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten mg... no, sorry, five mg. One tablet every morning, by mouth.

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Last winter, or the one before. Don't ask me which, I cannot remember.

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Ecosprin. Aspirin, the small white one.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): What strength, and is it every day?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Seventy-five mg. They told me once a day, but I take it on and off only, whenever I remember.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): You miss doses, then.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Many days I skip it. I am tired, don't lecture.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?

[SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Brendan? In you come. I put you on the machine on the way past, blood pressure was 138 over 82 and the pulse was 76. Doctor Walsh has your GP's letter about the cough.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand, thanks. It's not an emergency or anything, I just can't shake this cough, and the wife said I was to stop putting it off.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sit yourself down, Brendan. I'll hear it from you rather than the letter. How long have you had the cough?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks, solid. It came on the back of a dose of the flu. I was rotten for about a week, fever and aches and the whole production, and then that faded and the cough just... stayed.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): So the fever and the aches themselves have settled?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Settled, yeah. I was back in work after ten days. I'm a stores supervisor in the hardware place in Naas, so there's a fair bit of lifting, and I was able for that once the flu lifted. It's purely the cough now.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): When is the cough at its worst?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Night-time, no question. I'll be just dropping off and up it comes, a dry tickle, and I'm awake for ages. The wife has moved into the spare room, which tells you... anyway. Mornings there's a small amount of white phlegm, and then it's dry the rest of the day.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any blood in that phlegm?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have looked, more than once, and there's nothing red in it at all. And it's not a pain in the chest the way a heart pain would be, more a soreness across the front from the hacking itself.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever now, or proper night sweats, the drenching kind?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): The dog has me out the door at half six, rain or shine, down the canal and back, so the mornings are busy. Sorry, I went off on myself there. What was it you asked?
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fever, or night sweats.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever since the flu went. I get a bit clammy when the cough wakes me, but the sheets aren't wet. It's not that drenching kind of sweat.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): And are you breathless with it?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. The canal walk is grand and the yard is grand. I'm not gasping or anything like that.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Has your weight or your appetite fallen off?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No weight loss. The appetite is as good as ever, the wife still does the full dinner and I clear the plate. I haven't been near a scales, but I don't think I've lost any.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you been abroad lately, or around anyone with tuberculosis?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Abroad, no. I haven't left the country in years, the last holiday was Kerry and that was before Covid. TB, no, I don't know a soul with that. My brother was in Spain in May, but that's his holiday, not mine, I wasn't with him.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you on, including anything from the chemist?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Ramipril five milligrams, one in the morning, for the blood pressure, and I'm on that five years. The GP gave me clarithromycin, five hundred milligrams twice a day for five days, and I finished that about two weeks ago, it did nothing for the cough. At night I take ten mils of Benylin dry cough from the chemist, just to get over.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies I should know about before I...
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Penicillin. I came out in a rash all over when I was seventeen, and they told me not to take it again, so the GP wouldn't give me the usual antibiotic, that's why it was the clarithromycin. I've steered clear of penicillin ever since.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or did you?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. My father smoked forty a day and I couldn't stick the smell of it in the house, so I never started. I take a pint of a Saturday and that's the height of it, I'm not a drinker.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me have a listen to your chest. Deep breath in... and out. And again for me.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): The lungs are clear, I don't hear any crackles. There's a little wheeze right at the end of the breath, on both sides. Your throat looks ordinary, and there are no glands up in the neck.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Is the wheeze a bad sign? I have noticed a bit of a whistle at night when I'm lying down, I was going to mention that and then I forgot, the way you do.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Six weeks on from a flu, worse at night, a bit of phlegm in the morning, and that wheeze. My head runs through a post-viral cough, a twitchy airway, even reflux, and TB does cross my mind when a cough drags on like this. I'm not naming any of those as the cause. I want to see a chest x-ray before I commit to a thing.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): The x-ray, do I keep the jumper on or... oh, actually, the trousers. I said I hadn't lost weight, but I've gone in a notch on the belt and the waist is loose, I only copped it getting dressed this week. So I have lost a bit, I was wrong earlier.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): That detail matters, and we'll hold it alongside the film. I'm still not putting a name on this.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): And listen, I said no TB, and that's true as far as contact goes, I haven't been near anyone with it. My sister Niamh rang last week going on about our cousin Declan down in Limerick, he was in the hospital with a bad chest and she has it in her head that it was TB. I haven't laid eyes on Declan since a wedding in twenty nineteen, so I wouldn't call that contact.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): So a cousin with a chest illness your sister thinks was tuberculosis, and no contact yourself. I'm still not calling this TB, or calling it anything else. The picture has to come first.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll order a chest x-ray, today if they can fit you in. Keep taking the ramipril as you are, and the Benylin at night is fine if it helps you sleep. I won't be starting any new tablet until we've seen the film.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): And if it's something bad on the x-ray, what then? The wife will ask me the minute I get in the door, she has herself half convinced it's desperate, and I keep telling her it's probably nothing.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Then we deal with whatever the picture shows, not with a guess from me today. If you cough up blood, or you become properly breathless, or a fever comes back, don't wait on the appointment, go to the emergency department or the on-call GP. I'll see you back here in two weeks with the result.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, grand. I'll tell the wife, she'll be glad someone is actually looking at it instead of us arguing over it at the kitchen table.
[SEG0039] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Radiology can take him at half two, so I'll book the chest x-ray and the two-week review on the way out.

[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Um, it's me lower back, doctor. Been sore.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is it an ache, or does it catch?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Dull ache, and it catches if I bend. I don't know, doctor, words aren't my strong suit.
[SEG0006] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's been groaning getting out of the ute. Proper weeks of it.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Where do you feel it?
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): Low, belt-line, more on the right side. Not between the shoulders.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any pain running down the leg?
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Stays in the back, maybe a bit in the right bum. That's it.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has it been there?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): A few weeks. Or, well, actually, since the move. I don't know, doctor, I can't lock in a date.
[SEG0013] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The move was the start of March, so six weeks. He was lumping boxes the whole weekend.
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, call it six weeks then. I still couldn't tell you the first morning.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Righto, about six weeks, the actual day uncertain. I'll go through the serious features separately so we don't blur them.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness, pins and needles, or weakness in the legs, or around the groin and saddle?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Um, last Tuesday I was stood on the concrete for hours and the right foot went pins and needles. It came good once I walked to the smoko room. I don't know if that counts, doctor. It's not there today, and I don't reckon the back did it.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sounds like the foot simply went to sleep. So is there numbness now, or a leg that's weak?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No numbness now, no weakness.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about the bladder, leaking, trouble starting, not feeling the urge?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): No, bladder's normal. No worries there.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weight loss you weren't trying for?
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. I thought the belt was on a looser hole, but we've ditched takeaway while the kitchen's unpacked, and I haven't weighed myself. I don't think I've lost weight.
[SEG0024] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He hasn't. Same old jeans.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll record no unintentional weight loss. Any fever, chills, or night sweats?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): No fever, no sweats. I get whacked after a shift, but that's just the warehouse, not illness.
[SEG0027] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Off topic, but my mum takes metformin for her diabetes, has done for years, and Dave's sister chews biotin gummies for her hair. I keep thinking he needs a supplement. Silly, probably.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your mum's metformin and his sister's biotin aren't his medicines, so they stay off his list. A supplement won't sort mechanical pain. Dave, what are you actually using?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Panadol from the chemist. Two of the five hundred milligram tablets in the morning, and two more after work if the ache is up. If I'm okay I skip the arvo dose. I don't know, doctor, I just follow the box.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies, rashes, swelling with medicines?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Never had one. I don't know of any allergy.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the job.
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): Picker in a warehouse. Lifting cartons, some around twenty kilos, on my feet for an eight hour shift. Been doing it for years.
[SEG0034] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And we just moved to a rental in Footscray, so there were house boxes on top of that.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's have a look. Bend forward. You halt around mid-thigh, and the right lower back muscles are tender. Straight leg raise is comfortable, no pain down the leg, and the feet are strong.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, the bend is rotten. Lying flat on the floor settles it, a hot shower helps, and the wheat bag at night.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Score out of ten when it's bad?
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Maybe a six. Quiet days are more like a three. It chops and changes.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, thinking it through out loud. No red flags for cauda equina, infection, or something sinister. My working impression is a mechanical low back strain related to the lifting, present for six weeks. I can't completely rule out a small disc irritation because it's lingered, but nothing on today's exam shows a trapped nerve, so that stays unlikely.
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Gaz from work had a scan and a back op and he still can't lift. Am I heading there? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't put you in Gaz's boat. No scan today. A plain X-ray won't earn its keep here, so I'm not ordering one. We might arrange an MRI if this hasn't settled in a fortnight.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stick with the Panadol, two five-hundred milligram tablets morning and again after work only when you need them. Don't start your sister's biotin or your mother-in-law's tablets. Cut back the heavy cartons if the boss allows, keep walking, stay out of bed all day. If you can't pass urine, if numbness comes and stays, or if you get a fever with much worse pain, get seen the same day, emergency for the bladder.
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): Right. So I just wait and see?
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in two weeks, Jen can book it, so I can recheck the movement. If it hasn't eased by then, that's when we might go ahead with the MRI.

[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks is fine. Should I call sooner if I slide again?
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you actually pass out, or you fall and can't get up, go to the emergency room. Otherwise I'll see you in two weeks.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. And tell your nurse thank you for the blood pressure, even if the numbers were annoying.

[SEG0001] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hello, can I just check, is it Mrs Pickering, Joan Pickering? ~
[SEG0002] person_1 (PATIENT): It is, dear, Joan, born in the very same village as the doctor's mother, I'd wager. This is my Helen. ~
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hi. Mum's been dizzy since they changed her blood pressure tablets, that's why we're here.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Dizzy how, Joan?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): When I stand up, the room goes round and I have to hold the sideboard. It's been going on a while, a fortnight, perhaps longer, I couldn't tell you.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It was before Easter, wasn't it? Or after. I can't be sure either, honestly.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's fine. What does the dizziness feel like?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Light-headed, as if I might faint. I haven't, but it's close.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything with your vision?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): It goes blurry for a few seconds when I get up.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had any falls?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Not yet, touch wood.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): No pain in the chest.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Palpitations?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No, my heart's quiet as a mouse.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Headaches?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No headaches, no.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which tablets has she got now, Helen?
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ramipril, 10 mg, once a day. Amlodipine, 10 mg, once a day, that's the new one. And indapamide, 1.5 mg, in the morning.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. Any allergies, Joan?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Codeine, when I was a girl. It made me terribly sick. I've avoided it ever since.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Other health problems?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): High blood pressure, and arthritis in my hands.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Surgery?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): A hysterectomy, in 1985.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Family illnesses?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): My mother had a stroke.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Who's at home?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): I live with Helen and her husband now, since the stairs got too much.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): And before you retired?
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She was a seamstress for forty years.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me check your pressure lying down first. Blood pressure lying is 148 over 84.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Good. ~
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now stand up for me, slowly. Take your time. Standing, it's 108 over 64, and your pulse is 78.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, I do feel odd. ~
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sit down, Joan. That's quite a drop. Temperature is 36.5, oxygen 97 percent, and your weight is 62 kilos.
[SEG0038] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Is that bad? ~
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): It explains the dizziness. Let me listen to you.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Heart sounds are normal, and the lungs are clear.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Good. ~
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's no swelling in the ankles, and the mouth looks a little dry.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't drink as much as I should. ~
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with your breathing, Joan?
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing, I'm fine for breath.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): The blood pressure is dropping too low when you stand, which looks like the new tablet, but I can't rule out you being dried out as well.
[SEG0047] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): What happens now? ~
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to arrange an ECG, a blood test for kidney function and salts, and a urine test.
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): All today? ~
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. I'd also like to fit a 24-hour blood pressure monitor.
[SEG0051] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll bring her back for it. ~
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Drink plenty, stand up slowly. I'll decide about the tablets once I've seen the results, so please change nothing for now.
[SEG0053] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Understood. ~
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in two weeks.
[SEG0055] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks, dear. Lovely to meet you. ~

[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She has to stop halfway up the stairs at home. I filled the pill box this morning and I still don't trust it, so I came with her.

[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): Swelling of both legs for a month, worse by evening and a bit better with the feet up, breathless on the stairs the same length of time, two pillows, no chest pain and no cough. [SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): The water tablet is furosemide, the letter says twenty milligrams and the box says forty, so that dose is not agreed. [SEG0066] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's fair. What are you going to do?
[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): My impression is provisional, that fluid is building up again from the heart failure, and the dizziness might be the tablets or just standing up too fast, I can't separate those yet. [SEG0068] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The dizziness was there before I added the night one. It was only four days, and the old bottle is in the bin since this morning. She needs the blood pressure tablet, Dr Brennan was very firm about it.
[SEG0069] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right. I won't stop the ramipril. Stay on five milligrams once every morning, and nothing of it at night.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): I wanted to talk about my eating. I've been restricting a lot, and my friend said I should speak to someone.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you for telling us. That took courage. Can you tell me what restricting looks like for you?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): I skip breakfast and lunch most days, and I only have a small dinner. I count everything.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has it been like this?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): About one year. It got worse after exams last summer.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you been making yourself sick, or using laxatives?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Never. I just don't eat.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How do you feel about your weight and body? ~
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): I feel too big, even though people say I'm thin. ~
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you for being honest. Are you on any medicines?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Just the contraceptive pill, I think it's Microgynon, but I'm not sure.
[SEG0012] person_3 (NURSE): Doctor, I've weighed her and taken her pulse. Weight 46 kilos, height 165, pulse 54. ~
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. That's a low pulse, and a body mass index around seventeen.
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that bad? ~
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's lower than I'd like. Your body is working hard to protect you. Have you had any dizziness or fainting?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Dizzy when I stand up quickly. Never fainted.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have your periods been regular? ~
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): They stopped about six months ago. ~
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any past medical conditions?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Asthma as a child. And anxiety, last year, but I was never treated.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any operations?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): My tonsils, when I was nine.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you drink alcohol or smoke?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): No. I never have.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to be honest with you. What you describe sounds like an eating disorder, and I'd like to arrange a proper assessment.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't want to be put in hospital. ~
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): We're not talking about that now. I'm going to refer you to the eating disorder team, and we'll run bloods and an ECG.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. I think I do need help. ~
[SEG0029] person_3 (NURSE): I'll book the bloods with you before you leave today. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): And I'd like to see you again in one week, so we can check how you're managing.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): One week. Thank you for not judging me. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit wherever's easiest for the back. You look wrecked, the pair of you. What's brought you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): The back. The lower back. It's been murder, and I'm sick of talking about it already.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's like a briar, doctor, and he's not sleeping. We moved house and he lifted every box himself.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Sheila, I can talk. It's been a few weeks. Or since the move. I can't put a date on it.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's alright. Sheila, when do you think it started?
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The move was six weeks ago. He was hunched the night we shifted the couch, and I'd say it's been six weeks solid.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah, that is not it. I was grand for a while after the move. This is a couple of weeks, not six. I'm not fighting about a couch.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the dates for now. Whereabouts is the pain, and what's it like when it's bad?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Low down, across the belt line. Dull, and then it grabs if I bend. Mornings are desperate.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it go down either leg?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. Can we not pick at that.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll park it. Any numbness, or pins and needles, in the legs or round the groin?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No numbness. The legs feel normal.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the waterworks. Any struggle to pass urine, any leaking, or not feeling when the bladder's full?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Bladder's the same as ever. That's not why I'm here.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you lost weight without trying?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Trousers are a bit slack. Not really, though. I'm just off the dinners.
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He picks at his food, but he's not wasting away. Appetite's gone with the pain, that's all.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever, night sweats, or shivering?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. I'm tired, not sick-sick. Don't write me down as a temperature.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tired since when?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Since the back got bad. I'm not sleeping on it. I'm wrecked the whole day.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's up half the night pacing the kitchen, then into the warehouse for seven. And he's been at the tablets.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, warehouse operative. On my feet, lifting all day. They haven't a light duty between them, so don't bother suggesting it.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you taking, and what strength?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen from the chemist. I nearly said the two hundred milligram, but no, it's the four hundred milligram ones. Three times a day.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you get the three doses into you, and are you taking them with food?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly with food. I take them. Well, I miss the odd one, I'm not a robot.
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The middle-of-the-day one, he misses that half the time. I've seen the blister pack.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): It is not half the time. The odd one. I'm sat right here, Sheila.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else for the pain?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol as well, for a while. Two of the five hundred milligram tablets, four times a day. Stopped them last week. Useless.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Operations in the past, or any long-term illness?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No operations. The same spot in the back gave a twinge five-ish years ago and then it settled. Nothing else ongoing.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Smoking, or drink?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't smoke. Never did, really. A few pints at the weekend normally. Not this month, I'm too sore and too tired.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's just the two of us in the house. The kids are grown and gone, so it's me keeping an eye.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you're with him. I'm going to press along the low back. Say where it's worst.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): There. Right side. For God's sake, that's enough poking.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): The muscles either side of the low spine are tender, and it's clearly worse on the right. The bone itself isn't sore when I tap it.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Straight leg raise is clear on both sides, no pain shooting down. Power and feeling in the feet are normal. You can sit.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Finally. If I'm sweating it's from standing, not a fever. I already said that.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Noted. In the chair your blood pressure was one hundred and thirty-six over eighty-two, the pulse was seventy-four, and the temperature is thirty-six point six.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't come in about blood pressure. Is the back knackered or not?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pressure's fine. This fits a mechanical strain of the low back from the lifting. That's my working impression, not a final label, until we see how it behaves.
[SEG0048] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He has himself told it's broke. Does he not need a scan, doctor?
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): I said it feels broke. I did not say it is broke. Give over, the two of you.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): I don't think it's broken, and no scan today. If it's not settling in six weeks, we might arrange a plain x-ray of the lumbar spine.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. I've had enough weeks. Brilliant.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stay on the ibuprofen, four hundred milligrams three times a day, and take it with food every time. You can add the paracetamol back if you want, one gram four times a day, and don't go over those amounts.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep moving, short walks, and heat is fine if it eases you. Don't stay in the bed all day, and no heavy lifting in the warehouse until this settles. I know that's easier said.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Work will love that. I'm not after a sick cert, I'm not that man. And if I lie down tonight, I'm lying down.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): A lie-down is fine, it's all day in the bed that seizes you up. Come back sooner if the pain shoots hard down a leg, or you go numb, or the bladder changes. If it's not better in a fortnight, book back in with me.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight, then. I'm going home. Don't tell me to be positive about it. Thanks, I suppose.

[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me how it is now.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): My neck's stiff, especially in the mornings, and I get a pain across my shoulders by the afternoon. Worse after driving.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long is it since the accident? ~
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Four months. It was better at two months, then it plateaued. ~
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is the pain going down your arms, any numbness or tingling?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing in my arms. No tingling.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you using for the pain?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Naproxen, 250 mg, twice a day, maybe? And paracetamol, 1 gram, but I only take that when it's bad, so not every day.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. So 250 mg twice a day, as you recall it, and the paracetamol only when it's bad. Remind me of your history.
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): High blood pressure, a stomach ulcer, years ago, and my back's not great. Slipped disc.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had any operations?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): An operation on my lower back, a discectomy, in 2014.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you working?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I'm a delivery driver. Hours in the van.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look at your neck. Sit on the couch. ~
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tender over the muscles on both sides of the neck, tight and knotted in the upper shoulder muscles, and the movement is limited when you look over your shoulder.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that normal for four months on? ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's common. Whiplash can take months to settle, and the muscles tighten and guard. I'd say this is a persisting whiplash strain.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it ever clear? ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Most people recover, usually by six months, but you need to keep the neck moving. ~
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): I've been scared to. ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): I understand. Gentle exercises and physiotherapy help most. I'd like to arrange a referral for physio.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): When? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): A few weeks. Meanwhile, I'd like to arrange an X-ray of the neck, to be thorough, given the time that's passed.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Also, naproxen and your old stomach ulcer don't mix well, so please always take it with food.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): I've been taking it on an empty stomach, I'll stop. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take it only with food, and if you get stomach pain, or black stools, stop it and ring us. ~
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. Thank you. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Use a warm pack, and break up your driving with stops to stretch.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the pain spreads into your arm, or you get weakness or numbness in your hands, come back that day.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. Thanks, doctor. ~

Transcript (encounter 00555)
[SEG0001] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good morning. I have Odalys Ferreira on my screen. Did I say that right?
[SEG0002] person_1 (PATIENT): Close enough! It's Fer-RAY-ra, but I answer to anything. My own mother mangles the Portuguese half of the name.
[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fer-RAY-ra, got it. I'm covering for Dr. Haldane today, so I'm reading your chart as we talk. What brings you in?
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): Mostly my regular check on the HIV. Nine years now, and it's been so well behaved I almost forget about it.
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): The receptionist also said to mention an allergy thing, because the pharmacy flagged my chart.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Happy to get to that. First, how has the last stretch been for you?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Boring, which I'm told is the goal. Oh, but I parked in the wrong garage today, walked into the dental office across the street, and sat there ten minutes before anyone asked why.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha. Did they at least offer you a free cleaning?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): A pamphlet about flossing. That was the whole reward.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair trade. And your routine has been steady, even through the summer?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Mostly. I left my bag in a cab at my cousin's wedding in June, with everything in it. Got it back that evening and the driver wouldn't take a tip.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): What a relief. Okay, the allergy. What exactly did the pharmacy flag?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): My chart just says the word sulfa, nothing next to it, and they wanted to know what actually happens to me.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good question. So what does happen?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm allergic to sulfa drugs. I get a rash all over, and the last time my lips puffed up too.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's a serious reaction. When did you first find out?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Years ago, before the HIV diagnosis. I got an antibiotic for something minor and by day three I looked like I'd been dipped in strawberry jam.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Dipped in strawberry jam. Vivid. Did anyone ever test you, or is it simply what happened?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Just what happened. A dermatologist took photos and wrote sulfa in my file. She was thrilled, honestly, said it was textbook.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did she say whether the lip swelling changes how careful people need to be?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): She said that was the part that mattered. The rash is a nuisance, but swollen lips means you tell every doctor before they write anything.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): She's right. Some of the antibiotics used for people living with HIV are in the sulfa family, so the label matters even more for you.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): That's what the pharmacist said. We ended up chatting about her kid's science fair for twenty minutes.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): A pharmacist who chats. Keep her. Do you carry anything that says what you react to?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): A medical bracelet. My sister bought it, engraved and everything. Sulfa allergy on one side, emergency contact on the other.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Please keep wearing it. Now, mind if I listen to your chest and feel your neck?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Go ahead. Fair warning, I'm ticklish.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll be brisk. Deep breath in, and out. Once more.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your chest is clear, and everything feels normal in the neck.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): That's the answer I wanted. Do I get a gold star?
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Gold star, yes. Honestly, everything I see and hear today fits with your HIV being well controlled.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Which is boring. I'll take boring. My neighbor says I'm the most uneventful person on the street.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Uneventful is a compliment in this building. Anything you're unsure of with the allergy itself?
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Should I do anything different on my end?
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep the bracelet on, and tell any new doctor or dentist about the sulfa allergy before they prescribe anything, whatever you're there for.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Even the dental office I wandered into by accident?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Especially them. They might still have something for you.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Ha. I'll bring up the flossing pamphlet.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do. I'm going to update your chart so it reads sulfa drugs, with a rash all over and lip swelling, in your own words.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Perfect. The pharmacist will probably do a little dance.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd pay to see that. Anything else on your mind?
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Just a question. Is travel okay? My sister is getting married in Lisbon next spring.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Travel is fine for someone doing as well as you. Bring a short letter about the allergy, in English and Portuguese if you can.
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): My mother can translate it. She'll enjoy being useful.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): There you go. Congratulations to your sister in advance.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you. I'll be sure to dance at that one.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think that covers it. Watch which garage you pick on the way out.
[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): Third level, I promise. Thanks, doctor.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take care, Ms. Ferreira.
