[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr Brennan, in you come. The spirometry is done, I'll read it out when you're ready, doctor.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand, one second, this screen is after freezing on me again. Right. What has you in, Mr Brennan?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): The cough, mostly. Mornings are desperate, I'm hacking before the kettle's even boiled. And I'm breathless on the hill up from the shop. Mad rain all week, the collie next door won't step out in it.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long is the cough going?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Years, sure, always a morning thing. It's worse since the chest infection though, that was three weeks... no, five weeks ago. I was in bits.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? The screen jumped. Five weeks?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Five weeks, yeah. Fever and green phlegm, the lot. They gave me amoxicillin and I finished the course. Fever's gone, and the green stuff cleared.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with the breathlessness?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): No pain. And no blood, before you ask. Just the puffing and the cough.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): On the flat, or only on the hill?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Flat I'm grand enough. The hill to the house, I'm stopping halfway to get my breath. Yer man with the collie thinks I'm only nosing at his gate.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Is the phlegm still there in the mornings?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): A bit of white stuff, yeah. Not green anymore.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any wheeze?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): A small bit at night, if I'm lying flat. Not every night.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the smoking. How many are you on?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): About ten a day... ah, maybe twenty, if I'm straight with you. Since I was sixteen. Forty-odd years of it.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Twenty a day, a long time. Did you ever try stopping?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): The patches, last year. Itched the skin something awful, so I gave them up after a couple of weeks. Dear old things too, from the chemist.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you using inhalers?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): The blue one, salbutamol, when I need it. Some days that's four or five times. And the brown one, beclomethasone I think, two puffs... no, one puff, twice a day. I'm shocking for forgetting it.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Say the brown one again, I didn't catch the name.
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): Beclometasone. One puff twice a day, the days I remember. Maybe three or four days in the week, if that.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): So not every day.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): No. It lives in the drawer more than in my pocket, I'll admit.
[SEG0026] person_1 (NURSE): Will I give you the spirometry now?
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Go on, yeah.
[SEG0028] person_1 (NURSE): FEV1 was one point eight litres, sixty-two percent predicted. FVC three point one litres, eighty-one percent. Ratio nought point five eight.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): One point eight, sixty-two percent. Hang on, I'm typing it in. What about the observations?
[SEG0030] person_1 (NURSE): Saturation ninety-five percent on room air. Pulse eighty-eight. Blood pressure one thirty-eight over eighty-four. Breathing eighteen a minute. Temperature thirty-six point seven.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. I'll have a listen to the chest if you sit forward.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Work away. Mind the shirt, it's the good one. The wife ironed it before she went to her sister's in Cork, so I'm on beans on toast all week.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Breath sounds are reduced at both bases, and I've a few wheezes on the right. No crackles.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Is that desperate news, doctor?
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): It fits with the smoking and the tight airways. I'd call it a working diagnosis of COPD. The infection looks settled.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): COPD. My brother had that. Ended up on the oxygen. He smoked more than me, mind.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergy to medicines?
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Not that I know of. The amoxicillin was grand, no bother at all.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): The beclometasone we've got down here is two hundred micrograms. Is that the inhaler at home?
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): That's the one. Little brown thing, two hundred.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): I want that every day, one puff twice a day, not just when you remember. Keep the salbutamol for the breathlessness, two puffs when you need it.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): I'll try. The blue one I do use. The brown one slips the mind.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): We might do a chest X-ray if the cough does not settle. And let's see you in two weeks, see how the regular inhaler is going.
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): Two weeks is grand. Do I need to be fasting? Last time I was in for bloods they left me sitting an age, and I'd had no breakfast.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): No fasting. It's just the cough and the breathing we'll be looking at. I'd like to refer you on to the stop-smoking service, if you'll go.
[SEG0046] person_3 (PATIENT): Ah I suppose I should. Twenty a day isn't clever and I know it.
[SEG0047] person_1 (NURSE): I can book the cessation clinic from out here, doctor, if you want.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Book it, please. And the review here in two weeks.
[SEG0049] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put the two of them in.
[SEG0050] person_3 (PATIENT): Is the cessation one in this building or the other one? I get lost over there, the signs are useless.
[SEG0051] person_1 (NURSE): It's here, Thursday mornings as a rule. I'll give you the slip on the way out.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the breathing gets worse before then, or you're feverish again, don't wait the two weeks. Come back sooner, or go to the emergency department.
[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): I will, yeah. The wife would have my head if I left it. She's home Sunday.
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. We'll leave it there so.
[SEG0055] person_3 (PATIENT): Thanks, doctor. That computer's as slow as myself on the hill.
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about it. Mind yourself, Mr Brennan.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hi. Um, it's the anxiety. It's been bad again. I can't switch my head off at night.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me what happens at night.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): I get into bed and my mind races. Work, money, everything. I lie there for two hours, then wake at four, and I'm back on the treadmill.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has it been like this?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): About six weeks. Since I changed jobs.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any physical symptoms with it?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): My heart pounds, my chest feels tight, and I get sweaty hands. And I'm not eating much.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any panic attacks, or thoughts of harming yourself?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): A couple of panic attacks, on the train. But no, no thoughts of harming myself.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you taking at the moment?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Sertraline, 50 mg once a day. I've been on it three months.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is it helping? ~
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit, in the daytime. Not at night. ~
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other conditions?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): I had depression, years ago.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any operations?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Wisdom teeth out, three years ago.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you have a drink to calm you down? ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): A glass of wine, a couple of nights a week. ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me check your pulse and blood pressure. ~
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pulse 88, blood pressure 124 over 78, temperature 36.6.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it high? ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Slightly fast, but normal. Any breathlessness, or chest pain that worries you?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): No, just tightness when I'm anxious. Nothing otherwise.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. I'd say this is a flare of your anxiety, on top of a big life change, with sleep suffering.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it go? ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): It usually settles with the right help. I'd like to arrange a blood test, to rule out something physical like your thyroid, and check your vitamin levels.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): And I'd like you to try a sleep routine, no screens an hour before bed, a notepad by your bed to write the worries down, and keep caffeine before noon.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): The notepad's a good idea. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm also going to refer you for talking therapy, cognitive behavioural therapy, which is very effective.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): How long's the wait? ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): A few weeks. In the meantime, there are breathing exercises on the practice website.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll look them up. ~
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in three weeks, to see how you're sleeping.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Three weeks. Thank you, doctor. ~

[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any rash, or difficulty swallowing your saliva?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): No rash. I can swallow, it just hurts.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you taking at the moment?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Just paracetamol, 1 gram, four times a day.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look at your throat. Open wide. ~

[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): For strep throat, ten days is the full course, to clear it and prevent complications. Finish it all, even if you feel better in two. ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is there anything about the antibiotic you'd like me to explain before we go on? ~
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): No, that's clear enough. ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pulse 82, temperature 37.6, oxygen 98 percent.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that all right? ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fine. A mild temperature, as expected. Rest, drink plenty, and use paracetamol for the pain. Salt-water gargles help too.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Can I go to work? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stay off until you've had two days of the antibiotic, and your fever has gone.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you can't swallow, drool, have a very stiff neck, or a one-sided swollen throat, come back at once.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in a week, if you're not completely better.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Thanks, doctor. ~

[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm putting in a referral to our behavioral health counselor, so the two of you aren't carrying this alone. The thyroid blood draw can happen today if the nurse is still around.
[SEG0046] person_1 (NURSE): I can walk him to the lab once you're finished. We're still drawing for a bit.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Mr. Hale, I want to see you in four weeks either way, not only if you feel worse. We'll look at the thyroid and only then talk about whether sertraline makes sense.
[SEG0048] person_4 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate the care you have taken with this.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Afternoon. My ankles swell by evening. Been going on a month. I thought I'd mention it.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Both ankles, or one?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Both. Worse after a day on my feet, gone by the morning.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any breathlessness, or waking at night short of breath? ~
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. ~
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): What tablets do you take?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Amlodipine, 10 mg once a day. And omeprazole, 20 mg once a day.

[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): About six weeks. They put it up from five. ~
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's useful to know. Let's check you over. Pulse, pressure and so on. ~
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Go ahead. ~
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pulse 74, blood pressure 130 over 80, temperature 36.6, oxygen 98 percent, breathing 14 a minute.
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that okay? ~
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's fine. Up on the couch, and let me press on your ankles. ~
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): It leaves a dent, doesn't it? ~
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, there's mild swelling around both ankles, and it dents when I press. Your calves are soft and not tender.
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it my heart? ~
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nothing I've found points to that, and your lungs are clear. I'm not going to put a name on it today. ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. What do we do? ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Put your feet up in the evenings, above hip height if you can, and don't sit with your legs crossed for long.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): I sit all day at work, mind. ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take a walk at lunchtime, and get up every hour. Compression socks can help, too. ~
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Do you want me to stop anything? ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today. Let's see how it settles with the leg raising. ~
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): And if it doesn't? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in three weeks.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Three weeks. Fine. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): And if one leg swells much more than the other, or becomes hot and painful, come in the same day.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Understood. Thanks. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take care. ~

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I stopped smoking when my daughter was born, that's twelve years now. A beer or two at a braai on the weekend, that's it. My neighbour's Weber packed up and he borrowed my grid, whole story, you don't want it.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Twelve years, and weekends only for the beer. Any diabetes, asthma, heart trouble, or operations?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No diabetes, no asthma, no heart trouble. They took my tonsils out when I was small, that's the only one. Appendix is still mine.

[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Use a decent cuff, morning and evening, for two weeks. Sit quietly for a few minutes first, write every number down, and bring the list. Nothing from the pharmacy for blood pressure in the meantime.

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Book back with me in two weeks with that list, and I'll complete the depot form then. No scan for the knee today. If it's still catching you on the stairs when you're back, we'll look at it again.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): I've just done her observations in the side room. Blood pressure is 118 over 74, pulse 98 beats a minute, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius, oxygen saturation 98 percent on air, and her respiratory rate is 16 breaths a minute. She's been talking the whole time.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lovely, thank you. Come on through, both of you. Tell me what's happened, in your own time.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Oh it's been rotten, doctor. We went to my cousin Priya's wedding, peach and cream flowers, very tasteful, though the DJ was stuck on Wham and I could have done without that. After the sit-down meal my tummy completely gave up.
[SEG0004] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's skipping the important bit. Prawn starter, then a chicken curry that had sat under the lamps for ages. I had the vegetable curry and I'm right as rain.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did the diarrhoea and the sickness actually start? A day would help, even a rough one.
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): I can't give you one, that's the maddening thing. Was the wedding last Saturday, or the Saturday before? I even said to him it was since Diwali or after, and then I remembered Diwali was weeks ago, so that's rubbish. The runs started the night of the wedding or the next morning, and I honestly could not tell you which.
[SEG0007] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I thought Saturday just gone, then I started doubting myself. I can't swear to the day either. Sorry.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, we'll leave the start date open rather than invent one. How many times have you been opening your bowels?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): I did try to count. Six, and then I lost the plot. Seven, eight, maybe nine today, all watery, brown, not bloody. And these cramps low down in my tummy, they come in waves. Oh, and the loos at that venue, don't get me started, there were only two for the whole marquee.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any black stool, or blood you might have missed? And have you vomited? Any fever?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): No blood and nothing black, I'm sure of that. No fever, I don't think so. I felt a bit warm last night but I'm not today, and that might just have been their tropical heating. Vomiting, um, twice or three times, yesterday probably, and I'm still queasy now.
[SEG0012] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It was three times, all yesterday, over the kitchen sink. Nothing today. She's nauseous, not actually being sick.
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): Fine, three. He was counting, I was busy. Still got the nausea though, proper queasy, and those cramps haven't let up.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has anyone else from the wedding been poorly?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes, quite a few. My cousin's husband texted, same thing, and Auntie Meena, and a friend of theirs in a red hat whose name has fallen out of my head. So it's not just my constitution. The hat was a bit much, if I'm honest, for a wedding.
[SEG0016] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Three others that we know of. Every one of them had the prawns.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, thinking it through out loud, this could be a viral gastroenteritis, norovirus does exactly this, or a bacterial one from the food, campylobacter or salmonella. Several people ill after the same meal makes a foodborne bug more likely than a one-off virus, but I am not going to call it definite food poisoning. I can't separate virus from bacteria on the story alone.
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): I nearly had the paneer. I knew that curry looked tired. Hindsight, eh.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): What have you taken for it?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Imodium. The lad at the chemist said not to, he said loperamide can trap a bug inside if other people are going down with it, and to stick to fluids. I took it anyway because I had a shift I couldn't drop. Two milligram capsules, two yesterday afternoon and one this morning.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like you to stop the loperamide now. If this is bacterial, slowing the bowel can hang on to the germs. The treatment is fluid, not Imodium, and I'll come back to how to drink it.
[SEG0022] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I did say the same as the chemist. She nodded and took them anyway.
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): I nodded and I still had to be on the desk. I'm the receptionist at the dental practice, Mr Shah's place, and you can't vanish to the loo every ten minutes when the waiting room's full of toothaches. I vanished anyway. It was embarrassing.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any regular medicines? And any allergies to medicines or anything else?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Ramipril, five milligrams, every morning, for my blood pressure. No allergies at all. I did try to cut salt after the practice nurse said so, then the wedding buffet undid it, which is typical.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): How much are you managing to drink, and how's the urine?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Not enough. Plain water makes the nausea worse, so I've had sips of lemonade. I've weed twice today, darker than usual, and my mouth's like sandpaper, really thirsty. When I stand up I go a bit spinny. I haven't fainted, I just grab the doorframe.
[SEG0028] person_1 (NURSE): For what it's worth she kept a few sips of water down with me in the waiting room and she didn't vomit there. Pulse of 98 fits with being a little dry, but she was alert and chatting.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look. Your lips and tongue are dry. Tummy's soft, mildly tender across the lower abdomen, no guarding and no rebound, so nothing there is suggesting peritonitis. Putting that with the pulse and the poor urine, I'd call this mild dehydration, not enough to need a drip.
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): Good, because my neighbour had a drip for a tummy bug last winter, or it might have been the winter before, I lose whole years. I don't fancy a drip. She still talks about the sandwich they gave her afterwards, which is a strange thing to remember.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): No drip today. You're alert, you've kept some sips down, and the numbers aren't scary. What will sort the dehydration is proper oral rehydration, not lemonade on its own.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Mum swears by flat lemonade. She turned up with a bottle this morning and then we got onto the wedding cake, three tiers, and the top one was dry, which is ironic given the state of me.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Flat lemonade isn't oral rehydration solution. Please get Dioralyte or a similar sachet, one sachet in 200 mils of water, and sip it little and often, including after each loose stool. If you start vomiting every sip back, if you can barely pass urine, if you feel properly faint, or if you see blood, that's A&E, especially out of hours.
[SEG0034] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll pick the sachets up on the way home. Is she allowed to eat?
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Small bland things if she fancies them, toast, rice, a banana. Nothing spicy, and don't force a meal. And the Imodium stays stopped.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): My cousin said they sent a sample of his. Should you not test mine?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not sending a stool sample today. If this hasn't clearly settled in three days, or if blood appears, then we send a culture. A result this afternoon wouldn't change the fluids and the waiting, so I won't pretend it would.
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): I was rather hoping you'd just switch it off. Some tablet that stops it dead.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): I know the feeling. Antibiotics aren't the right move on this story, not without blood, a high fever, or a sample that says so. Most of these burn out if you replace the fluid. I'm still leaving virus versus bacteria open.
[SEG0040] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Should she still take the ramipril if she's dried out? Five milligrams feels like a lot when she's not drinking.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep the ramipril, five milligrams each morning, as long as she's taking fluid and not fainting. If she can't keep fluid down, hold the tablet and ring the surgery. I'm not changing the dose today.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): It makes me cough, that one, sometimes, and it's done it for ages. Is that even related? Also I've not been abroad, before you ask, just Leeds for the wedding. My passport expired in a drawer, whole other drama.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, ramipril can give a dry cough. I'm not swapping it in the middle of a gastroenteritis. Mention it when you're next seen about your blood pressure. We haven't booked that today.
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): So, fluids, no Imodium, wait and see. Can I work tomorrow? Mr Shah's doing implants all morning and the new girl still can't work the software. It'll be carnage without me, carnage of a different sort.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not tomorrow. Stay off until the diarrhoea is easing and you're keeping fluid down, a day or two at least. You're infectious while it's loose, so hand washing, and don't share towels. If you're worse tonight, go to A&E as I said. If it's not clearly improving in three days, book back in with me and we'll do that stool test.
[SEG0046] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll keep an eye on her tonight and I'll get the Dioralyte. Thank you.
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): Thanks, doctor. If the actual day suddenly comes back to me I'll ring, but I wouldn't hold your breath. Those peach flowers were lovely, though. Tell whoever does your waiting room they could learn from it.

[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): And what about weight loss or weakness?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No weight loss or weakness, none of it.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any palpitations or fainting?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Nope, nothing like that.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): How's your breathing otherwise?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Breathing's normal.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any health conditions I should have on record?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): I have heart disease, for about ten years. I have an irregular heartbeat.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): I see, go ahead. Okay, I can see heart disease and an irregular heartbeat in your file as well.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you taking anything regularly, including from the pharmacy?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): It's aspirin, once a day for my heart.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): And what strength is that?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): 75 milligrams, I think that's what's on the box.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): About two months. Bisoprolol, 2.5 milligrams, once a day.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm-hmm. A few questions about your lifestyle now.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): I live with my elderly mother. I do a yoga class on Thursdays. I'm vegetarian and have been for years.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any previous surgeries?
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, nothing, I haven't had any operations.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, now I'm going to do a short physical check.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): That's alright.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me feel here.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): There is a fine, fast tremor that goes away when the hands are resting.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's all I needed to check. Having listened and examined, my working impression is an anxiety or caffeine-related tremor. The reason I say that is that your story and my examination fit together. An overactive thyroid is still possible.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Is this permanent?
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): I understand the worry. At the moment I'd say it's an anxiety or caffeine-related tremor, and we'll know more once the a thyroid test is back. I'd like to arrange a thyroid test for tremor. Cut down caffeine and try slow breathing when it starts.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): I see, go ahead. Do get help quickly if the symptoms get worse. Come back in four weeks. So, that's everything on my side. Anything you're unsure about?
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): I think I understand everything. Thanks.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in. Sorry the waiting room was so full this morning.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, Doctor. Please do not apologise. I am grateful you could see me.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Of course. What brings you in?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I have a cough which has lasted six weeks. It came on after a bout of flu, and it has not cleared.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Six weeks is a fair stretch. Tell me about that flu, would you.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I was in bed for about ten days with a fever. That was, well, about eight weeks ago. The fever settled, but the cough did not.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the cough dry, or do you bring up phlegm?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): It is mostly dry, Doctor. In the mornings there is a small amount of clear phlegm. It is never coloured.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any blood at all?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have not coughed up any blood.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): When is it at its worst?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): It is much worse at night. I wake with it. It is present in the daytime as well, only less so.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your breathing?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I am a little short of breath on the stairs. On the flat I am perfectly all right. I do not wheeze.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever now, or sweats in the night?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever since the flu, and no night sweats. I feel quite myself in that regard.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has your weight changed?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I have not lost weight.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any travel abroad recently, or contact with anyone who has tuberculosis?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No recent travel. And no, I have not been in contact with tuberculosis.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): I have never smoked. I take one small glass of wine with dinner on a Saturday, and that is all.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you working at the moment?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I am retired. I left the Department five years ago.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand. Medicines, then. What do you take regularly?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Lisinopril, ten milligrams, by mouth, one tablet every morning, for my blood pressure. I have been on it for years.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else in the last while, even a short course?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): During the flu the out-of-hours doctor prescribed amoxicillin. He first said two hundred and fifty milligrams, then he corrected himself to five hundred milligrams, three times a day, for five days. I finished every dose. I am not taking it now.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough mixture or inhaler?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No inhaler. At night I take one spoonful, by mouth, of a brown cough bottle from the chemist. I am sorry, I cannot recall the name of it. It scarcely helps.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's fine. We won't guess the name. Does anyone at home take medicines that could be confused with yours?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): My wife takes metformin for her diabetes. I believe it is five hundred milligrams, but it is hers alone, and I have never taken it. My sister often urges me to try biotin, as she does, and I have not taken that either.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies to any drug?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): None. I have never had an allergic reaction.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any history of asthma, or anything else ongoing besides the blood pressure?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No asthma. The blood pressure is the only thing that continues. I should mention that about two years ago the hospital did a chest x-ray, and they said it was borderline, something to do with the size of the heart. Nobody followed it up with me.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, so we'll note that old film as borderline on heart size, without treating it as a firm result. The blood pressure is the condition we already know about.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, Doctor. That is correct.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stomach, waterworks, the rest of you, any trouble there?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Those systems are entirely in order.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Before I examine you, you look as if the morning has already been long.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Indeed. I left the house in plenty of time, and still the traffic on the N11 was at a standstill. I was twenty minutes just getting past the Bray turn.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): I came the same way. The rain has the whole of the coast road crawling. Did you see the state of the sky over the Sugar Loaf?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): I did. It was black as ink, and then a gap of blue for about five minutes, and then it closed over again. Very Irish, if I may say.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): My granddaughter was meant to have her school sports on the green this afternoon. I rang my daughter at breakfast and she said they have moved the whole thing into the hall.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): That is a pity for the children. My own grandson, Ciarán, had his hurling blitz cancelled last Saturday for the very same reason. He was dressed in the kit from half seven, and then the text came.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): How old is he now?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): He is eight. Mad for the hurling, and he supports Kilkenny, though the rest of us are Dublin. We had quite a debate about it over Sunday lunch.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Kilkenny will do that to a house. Was the lunch at yours?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): At my daughter's, in Rathmines. She made a roast, and the small fellow ate nothing but the potatoes. We stayed on for the crossword, which he is already better at than I am.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): They always are. I still buy the paper on a Saturday out of habit, and the sports pages are the only bit I finish.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): I do the same. I will not pretend I understand the cricket they put on the back page in summer, but I read it all the same. It is a harmless way to spend the evening.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Harmless indeed. Right. Shall we come back to yourself?
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Of course. Doctor, I ought to correct something I said: I told you I had not lost weight, but fastening my coat just now I saw I have taken the belt in a notch and the trousers are loose. I have lost some weight, and I could not tell you when that began.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you for putting that right. We will keep it in mind, though we cannot date it. Is there anything else?
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): One thing, if I may. I still do not believe I have had contact with tuberculosis, for I have not seen my cousin Declan since Christmas. My sister telephoned last week, though, and said he had been in hospital with a chest complaint. She thought it might be tuberculosis, but she was not sure, and it may only have been pneumonia.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): I follow you. We will not call that contact, and we will not put the name tuberculosis on it either, because nobody in this room actually knows. Let me examine you.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your blood pressure today is one hundred and thirty-eight over eighty-four. Your pulse is seventy-six, and it is regular.
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): The temperature is thirty-six point eight degrees. Your oxygen level is ninety-seven percent, and your breathing rate is sixteen.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): I think that is better than the chemist. They had me at around one hundred and fifty over ninety-five a month ago, though I did not write it down.
[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): We will use today's figures. The chest is clear. I do not hear crackles, and I do not hear a wheeze.
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): The throat is a little red. There are no swollen glands in the neck. The heart sounds are normal, and there is no murmur.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): I am glad the chest is clear. Does the redness matter at all?
[SEG0066] person_1 (DOCTOR): A little redness can linger after a viral illness. I am thinking this through out loud with you. A cough that goes on for six weeks can have a few explanations, and I am not going to put a name on the cause today. Naming one now would only be guessing.
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): I quite understand. I would sooner you were sure.
[SEG0068] person_1 (DOCTOR): What I will do is order a chest x-ray. It is to have a proper look, not because I have decided there is anything in particular on it.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): Will that be soon, Doctor?
[SEG0070] person_1 (DOCTOR): I will ask reception to arrange it this week. If the film shows something that needs a sample, I might send sputum then. I am not ordering the sputum today.
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): And as regards medicine? I did finish the antibiotic.
[SEG0072] person_1 (DOCTOR): I am not prescribing another antibiotic. It would not settle a cough of this sort at this stage, and I want the picture first. You may keep taking the spoonful of that cough bottle at night, though we do not know its name, and please do not start your wife's metformin or your sister's biotin.
[SEG0073] person_2 (PATIENT): I should never do that. What ought I to watch for?
[SEG0074] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you cough up blood, or the shortness of breath gets worse, or a fever returns, do not wait. Come back here, or go to the emergency department, the same day.
[SEG0075] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall do so. And when should I come back to you in the ordinary course?
[SEG0076] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks and we will go through the x-ray together. If the appointment for the film has not come through by Friday, ring the surgery and we will chase it.
[SEG0077] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. You have been very clear, and I am most grateful.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on back. I'm Dr. Ellison. Lap or table, Leo, your call. What brings you in?

[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): I won't stop you yet.
[SEG0004] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So the cold started two weeks—
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): I want a sticker.
[SEG0006] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): —ago? No, sorry, about ten days ago. Clear runny nose and a cough that was worse at night. The nose is mostly dried up, and the cough is still a little, mostly in the morning.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did the ear join in?
[SEG0008] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I almost said five days because I'm tired, but it's not. Friday night he woke up screaming, so three nights. He grabs the right ear and won't lay on that side, and daytime he's just cranky.
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): My ear doesn't hurt.
[SEG0010] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You say that now.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Daytime's different sometimes. Any fever with all this?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): I dreamed about a big truck. It was loud.
[SEG0013] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. I checked under the tongue, and he actually cooperates. It was ninety-eight point four yesterday and the same this morning. Grandma was over and she kept saying he felt hot, like she was completely sure.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): She thought it was a fever?
[SEG0015] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She was sure. I wasn't, the thermometer didn't agree, so I'm saying no fever.
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): I was hot. Grandma said hot potato. My pajamas were hot and the blanket was scratchy and I kicked it off and I was still hot and I wanted water.
[SEG0017] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He'll give you a whole paragraph. He felt warm to her hand, but the number was normal. I still say no fever.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Noted, both versions. Any drainage, like pus, from that ear?
[SEG0019] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No pus. I looked with a phone light, which is silly, but nothing was coming out.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hearing seem off at all?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): The truck dream had a horn.
[SEG0022] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Oh, hearing, sorry, he jumped in. No, he hears the TV even when I turn it way down. I meant to answer you and then I lost the question.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): All good. With the cough, any trouble breathing or wheezing?
[SEG0024] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No wheezing, just that leftover morning cough. He wheezed one time as a baby with a different cold, not now.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): What have you used for the pain?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): The pink medicine, strawberry but not a real strawberry, and I swallow it. I can tell you how the cup works, there's a line and Mommy says stop and one time I wanted to go past it. She said no, so I didn't, and then I asked why the line is there.
[SEG0027] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's the Tylenol, the children's red box, 160 milligrams in each 5 mL. I told my sister five mils and that was me misremembering, we fill the syringe to 7.5. Every six hours when he's crying, not around the clock, and it helps for maybe an hour. Sitting up on the couch is what really helps, and flat is worse.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else he's on, vitamins or drops?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): There was another pink one when I was little at Grandma's, and she tells the story every single time and it goes on and on and I just wait for it to stop.
[SEG0030] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's not a medicine now. When he was about fifteen months they gave him amox— I keep calling it Augmentin and that's wrong, it was amoxicillin, the pink liquid. For an ear, I think, or maybe his throat, long ago. He finished the bottle, I think.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any reaction to that amoxicillin?
[SEG0032] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I think he got a rash, maybe, a couple days into it. It could've been the virus, I honestly don't know. My mother calls it an allergy, and I was never sure enough to put it on a form. So maybe don't write allergic in stone.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Possible rash, not proven, so amoxicillin stays in the maybe column. Any foods or other drugs he can't have?
[SEG0034] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Not that I know of. No food stuff. I would remember hives.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Leo, I'm going to look in your ears with a little light. It stays on the outside.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Last time the light was cold and I said ow, but it was surprise not hurt. They had a brown dog sticker, not a cat, because Mason's cat scratches. I started telling the lady the whole cat story and she said honey we have to keep moving.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sticker after this, I promise. Let me see the right ear.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): The right eardrum is a little pink, the landmarks are still there, and it's not bulging. No hole and nothing draining. The left ear looks normal. Throat is clear with no pus, and the neck glands aren't swollen.
[SEG0039] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So is it infected? Don't soften it for me.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm working it through out loud. A cold swells the little drainage tube, fluid sits there, and lying down makes it throb. This could be a mild ear infection, or just pressure and fluid without much infection. I can't cleanly separate those on one look.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Is there a bug in my ear?
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): No bug, just irritation. His forehead isn't warm right now, but I didn't take a temperature in the room, so that's only my hand.
[SEG0043] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A few other things while he's quiet. He mentioned his tummy yesterday, then ate two waffles, so forget the tummy, and he's drinking milk and juice fine with a slightly lower appetite. Home is just the two of us, and he does preschool mornings where half the class is coughing. They pass colds around like snacks.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): I don't need to march through every other system. Drinking is the piece I cared about, and we'll leave the tummy if you're leaving it.
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): I didn't sleep. I waked up and the drum was going boom boom in my ear and I cried and Mommy came and my bear fell and I couldn't find him in the dark. My ear was really really hurting, not pretend, and I wanted the pink medicine and the couch, not the bed.
[SEG0046] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Every night since Friday, so yes, the ear hurts, he just won't say it until he feels safe. Nights are the bad part and days he mostly plays.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): So worse when he's flat, better sitting up, and Tylenol only takes the edge off. Did he ever actually swallow ibuprofen, the brown one?
[SEG0048] person_3 (PATIENT): The brown one is spicy and I spit it at Grandma's. She made a face and started the long medicine story, and I stopped listening when she said rash because rash stories are boring. I wanted a cracker instead and she said after the story, which is never after.
[SEG0049] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): One try, and he spit the whole thing, so I don't count a dose he didn't swallow. We can try again if you really want, but I know how that goes.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): No need to fight him over it. Keep the Tylenol at 7.5 mL every six hours only when he needs it, and don't wake him just to dose. [SEG0051] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): What about an antibiotic? Grandma already texted me a name, and I'm not freelancing that.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't start one today. It's been three nights, there's no fever we can document, the drum isn't bulging, and he's drinking. Plenty of these settle in a couple of days with pain medicine, so this is watchful waiting.
[SEG0053] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): If they don't settle, I need the back-up plan before I leave, or I'll spin on it at ten p.m.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll send a prescription today so it can sit at the pharmacy. Azithromycin suspension, 200 milligrams per 5 mL, give 5 mL by mouth once a day for three days. I'm staying off amoxicillin because of that possible rash. Don't pick it up today and don't start it today.
[SEG0055] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Azithromycin, once a day for three days, not the amox. When am I actually allowed to start it?
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): If he's not better in two days, come back and start the azithromycin. [SEG0057] person_3 (PATIENT): Can I get a sticker now, a dinosaur, because dinosaurs don't scratch? Mason's cat does, and at preschool they have goldfish crackers. One time the goldfish spilled all over the rug and everybody yelled and I still think about the crackers.
[SEG0058] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Dinosaur after the last bit, honey. Can you say the follow-up again so I don't invent a visit we don't need?
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Only if he needs you to come back. If he's himself again, just stay home. Most likely this is a mild ear infection we can watch, and leftover fluid from the cold is the other possibility I can't rule out. Either way I'm not starting an antibiotic in the room today.
[SEG0060] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Three nights already feels like a month, but okay, we'll wait. We'll keep the Tylenol and we won't start the other medicine unless it's the way you said. Thank you for not rushing it into his mouth.
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): You brought him at the right time. Leo, you were brave, and the sticker box is out front.
[SEG0062] person_3 (PATIENT): I'm telling Grandma there wasn't a bug. She'll still say hot potato, she always says hot potato, even when I eat a cold popsicle. One time the popsicle was red and it dripped on the couch and she still said hot potato.
[SEG0063] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll edit that story in the car. Thank you, Doctor.
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anytime. If the pain suddenly gets much worse before those two days, don't sit on it.
[SEG0065] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I won't. Come on, dinosaur sticker, then home.

[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): What antibiotic did they give you?

[SEG0036] person_3 (CAREGIVER): With the infection, about three weeks back, he was feverish and the phlegm was green for about a week. Then the amoxicillin, and he's been off it since Tuesday.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): That infection does sound as if it has settled. Do you have any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): None that I am aware of, Doctor.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'd like the brown inhaler used properly, please, two puffs of the two hundred microgram one, twice a day, every day, not only when you remember. The blue one stays two puffs as you need it, for the breathlessness.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall try to be more regular with it. I do apologise for being careless.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): No apology needed. About the cigarettes, would you like some help to stop? I can refer you to our stop-smoking service.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, please do. I think it is time. I am a little nervous about it, but I would like the support.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll ask reception to book that. And if the breathlessness is no better in six weeks, come back and see me. Sooner, obviously, if you cough up blood, or the fever returns, or you can't finish a sentence.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. Thank you, Doctor.
[SEG0045] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll move the brown inhaler to beside his toothbrush, morning and night. And I won't buy the cigarettes when I do the shopping.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): That would be a real help, thank you. Sister, is the blood pressure in the folder as well?
[SEG0047] person_4 (NURSE): Yes, Doctor. Earlier it was one thirty-six over eighty-two. Nothing else outstanding.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Mr Naidoo, use those inhalers as we've said, go along to the quit session, and come back if you're not easier in six weeks, or earlier if you worsen.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you very much for your time, Doctor. Good afternoon.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr Brennan, in you come. I'll grab a blood pressure before the doctor sees you. 136 over 84, pulse 58, and the scales have you at 89 kilos.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, that's grand. Sit yourselves down. What has you in?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): The tiredness, doctor, though if I start properly I'll wander. I do the accounts at the co-op, the month-end is a killer, I'm 53 in March, and I've been putting the whole lot down to the job and to getting older.
[SEG0004] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's asleep in the armchair before the nine o'clock news, most nights. I had to drag him in.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): I was getting to that. I couldn't tell you when the tiredness began — last winter, or the one before, one or the other. I'm no use after half four, and the backlog at work just sits there.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the fatigue's been there a good while, and you can't pin the start. Are you cold with it as well?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Freezing, even with the heating up and a jumper on in the kitchen. That's been the same stretch of time, whatever length it is, hands worst of all, and the weight —
[SEG0008] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry — the jumper is year-round. He had it on in June.
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): The weight, yes. You've me at 89. I was twelve stone a few years back, about 76 kilos, so that's the best part of two stone, and I haven't really changed the eating, only more tea and biscuits at the desk because the days run long.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weight up, cold, tired. What about the bowels, any change? And has your mood dipped, or is it just the energy?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): The bowels are a misery. Constipated, every three or four days, hard stools, and I'm after trying prunes and then senna from the chemist. The mood I'll come to, because the senna is a small saga in itself —
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): How much senna, and how long have you been on it?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): Two tablets at night, only the last fortnight, and it's done nothing. I read the packet twice so I wouldn't take the wrong amount, and I still feel blocked.
[SEG0014] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's been very flat as well, and the garden's gone to —
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): That's the mood you asked about. I'm low. No interest in the garden and I used to live out there. I don't think I'm depressed, I just put the flatness down to being wrecked from work.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Low, but not depression in your own view. Any thyroid trouble in the family?
[SEG0017] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His mother had the underactive thyroid, for years.
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Eltroxin, they called the tablets, right up until she died, God rest her. I think her sister might have had something similar but I never got that straight, so I won't swear to it. I had a blood test myself once and they told me it was borderline.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): When was that blood test?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): I couldn't date it if you paid me. Before the pandemic, or just after, or somewhere in between. They said borderline, I'm nearly sure of the word.
[SEG0021] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The letter said normal, Seán. It's in the sideboard at home. You've called it borderline for years and it wasn't.
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): Was it normal? I was certain they said borderline. Sure maybe I have it wrong — I do mix the old results up.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, we won't hang anything on that old result, since you remember borderline and your wife remembers a normal letter, and neither of you can date it. Let me say back what I have. Tired and cold since last winter or the winter before, weight from about 76 kilos up to 89, bowels every three or four days, mood low but not what you'd call depression, mother with an underactive thyroid, senna two at night for a fortnight with no joy.
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): That's the bones of it. I still think the co-op hours are half the story, mind you, and the age.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): They might well be. On examination your hands are cool, the pulse matches the 58 the nurse got, and I can't feel any enlargement or lump in the thyroid itself.
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): Is a normal feel a good thing? My mother had a goitre late on — or was that someone else. No, it was her, I'm sure of that much.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): A normal feel doesn't rule an underactive thyroid in or out. This could be hypothyroidism, or it could be the workload and age catching you, and I can't tell those apart from the chair.
[SEG0028] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So you'll do a blood test, will you?
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): I will. I'll order a thyroid function test, and a full blood count as well, with the tiredness gone on this long. Not this minute — the nurse will book the phlebotomy.
[SEG0030] person_1 (NURSE): Thursday morning is free, if that suits ye. I can put the form through now.
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Thursday morning is the audit, I can't do morning, the regional manager is in and I'll be stuck at the desk till lunch. Afternoon I could manage, if there's a slot, though the car park is desperate after three —
[SEG0032] person_1 (NURSE): Afternoon, so. Half two.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. Leave the senna off, since two at night for a fortnight hasn't shifted things. Plenty of water, and don't write the whole thing off as age until we have the numbers.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): If it is the thyroid, is it the same tablet my mother was on? I don't fancy being on something for life if I can avoid it, though I know people are, and she managed grand on it for years.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): We don't start any tablet until the result is back, and we'll talk it through then. Come back to me about a week after Thursday, once the results are in.
[SEG0036] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll root out that old letter so you're not depending on his memory of it.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Mr Bell. I'm Jess. I'll just grab your observations before Dr Rahman calls you. Could you pop your arm out?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning. Yes, of course. This one is quite alright.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Ta. Blood pressure is one thirty-eight over eighty-two, pulse seventy-six, temperature thirty-six point seven, and oxygen saturation ninety-eight percent.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. We were a little late, the traffic on Parramatta Road was dreadful.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Yeah, it's always a car park this hour. Doctor won't be long. There's water just there.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Arthur, Sandra, come in. I'm Dr Rahman. Make yourselves comfortable. What's brought you in?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, Doctor, and thank you for seeing me. I have a pain in my stomach, and I have been sleeping poorly.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry, that sounds miserable. Tell me about the pain in whatever way makes sense to you.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): It is a burning pain, just under the breastbone. It is moderate, and it comes chiefly in the evenings. It has been there since Diwali, or after Diwali. I cannot give you a firm date.
[SEG0010] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Sorry to jump in, I'm Sandra, I live in and look after him. He's playing it down. The pain's all day, he's hardly eating, and he's bringing his dinner back up.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Forgive me, I must correct that. I have not been vomiting. I am still eating, only smaller portions. And the burning is in the evenings, not all day.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): I hear you, Arthur. I'll take your own account of what you feel, and I've heard Sandra too. Does anything set the burning off, or settle it?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): A large meal makes it worse, and lying flat makes it worse. Warm milk eases it a little, and I sleep propped on two pillows.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): How have the nights been, then?
[SEG0015] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Two hours, if that. He's pacing the kitchen at three.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): That is more than the truth, I'm afraid. I do sleep, but I wake several times. It began last winter, or the one before. I cannot say which.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): When you wake, what's going on? The burning, or just wakefulness?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Frequently the burning. At other times I am simply awake. My mind is not especially troubled.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever with this? Black or tarry stools? Trouble swallowing?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. No black stools. I swallow perfectly well.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): And your weight, over this time?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, before I forget, the jacaranda out the front is lovely this week. Um, the weight, I have lost a little, though I have not been on the scales.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ha, they are lovely. A little weight down, without a number, that's fine. Are you on any medicines?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): I take two Panadol tablets, five hundred milligrams each, about three evenings a week, when the burning is bad. And amlodipine, ten milligrams... well, actually, five milligrams, every morning, for my blood pressure.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Five milligrams of amlodipine, got it. Anything else, Nurofen or ibuprofen from the chemist?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I do not take those. They have never suited my stomach.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. Any allergies to medicines, foods, anything?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): None at all. No known allergies.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): How about alcohol? Where does that sit for you?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Only socially.
[SEG0031] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Arthur, come on. It's a bottle most nights. I'm the one picking it up from the bottle shop.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, yes. I was too tidy about it. A bottle of wine most nights, perhaps. I apologise for the first answer.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): No apology needed, and no judgement. I'm glad you've told me. That much wine can stir up the stomach, and I'd like to know how your liver is coping. Do you smoke at all?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I have never smoked. Not even as a young man.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. And at home it's you and Sandra?
[SEG0036] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Just us. I do the cooking and the shopping, and I stay over. It's a live-in arrangement.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. It has suited me very well.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mind if I have a feel of your tummy? Hop up on the couch when you're ready.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Certainly. Shall I lie flat?
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, knees a bit bent if that's easier. Your abdomen is soft, tender just under the breastbone where I'm pressing, with no guarding. I can't feel any lumps, and bowel sounds are present.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that pressure is the place. It is not unbearable.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Putting this together, it may be gastritis, or it may be reflux. I can't tell those apart today. The evening meals and the wine could both be feeding it.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): I see. I had wondered if it was simply indigestion.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): It might sit in that family, yes. I'd like to start pantoprazole, forty milligrams, one tablet by mouth, every morning, half an hour before breakfast, for the burning.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall take it exactly so. Do I get it from the chemist?
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, I'll write the script. And I'll order liver blood tests today, because of the wine, to see how the liver is travelling. Jess can take the blood after we're done.
[SEG0047] person_1 (NURSE): I'll do the bloods straight after, no worries. Tubes are ready out the back.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): In the meantime, smaller evening meals, ease back on the wine if you can manage it, and stay propped up after dinner rather than lying flat. If you vomit blood, or the pain becomes severe and sudden, don't wait on me, go to emergency.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. I will be careful, and I will go to emergency if that happens.
[SEG0050] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll keep an eye, and I'll cut the wine down in the shopping.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): That would help. Come back in a fortnight and we'll go through the blood results. You're both welcome.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight. Thank you, Doctor. You have been very clear, and very kind.
[SEG0053] person_4 (CAREGIVER): We'll book it on the way out. Thanks.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on in and have a seat. I'll grab vitals while he's finishing up a note.

[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Enjoy it while it lasts. Date of birth, so I pull the right chart?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): March 12th, 1974. So fifty-one.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Perfect. Relax this arm. Blood pressure is one thirty-eight over eighty-two, and your pulse is 56.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifty-six? Is that too slow? I don't know. Sorry, you're the nurse, not the doctor.
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): It's on the slow side, not something I'd call urgent. Temperature's ninety-seven point four. Oxygen is 98 percent.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, I believe the low temp. I've been freezing.
[SEG0009] person_1 (NURSE): Step on the scale for me. A hundred and eighty-one pounds. Last weight we have is a hundred and sixty-four, and that was a couple of years ago.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I thought I'd gained like ten pounds... no, if I was 164, that's more like seventeen. Huh. I don't know.
[SEG0011] person_1 (NURSE): You taking any medicines every day?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Vitamin D. I almost said a thousand units, but the bottle's two thousand, once a day. Ibuprofen sometimes if my knees ache, not every day.
[SEG0013] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put that in. He should be right in. I've got to open the next room.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hey, sorry about the wait. This thing logged me out mid-sentence. One second... okay, I think it's back. What brings you in?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm just exhausted. Bone tired. I kept telling myself it's the job.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Say that again? Screen flickered, I lost the first half.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Tired. I'm wiped out when I get home, even on quiet days. It's been three months... no, that's wrong. It was already going on before the holidays, so more like eight months.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Eight months. You said eight? I want to type it right this time.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Eight. I don't know, doctor, maybe it's been creeping longer, but eight months is the honest answer.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): And work is what, exactly?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm a bookkeeper. Tax season about kills me every year, but this didn't ease up after April, so I can't pin the whole thing on April.

[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Cold all the time, or off and on?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Nurse has you at 181 today. You'd noticed the weight?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, nothing fits. I've been eating junk at my desk, and I'm fifty-one, so I blamed that.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about your bowels? Constipation, diarrhea, any change?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Constipation, yeah. I'm going maybe every three days and I have to strain. When it started, I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the stool?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I haven't seen any.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fevers?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): How's your mood through all this?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. I'm not depressed. It's not a mood thing, it's work and getting older.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hair thinning at all, or breaking more?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. Hard to tell.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that once more? A page popped up and the note scrolled on me.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Hair. I said sometimes, not really. I don't know.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll leave it blank then. Anybody in the family with thyroid disease? I'm asking because of the fatigue.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): My mom. She had thyroid disease and took some pill for years. I couldn't tell you the name. She died in 2018, not from the thyroid, from a stroke, I think.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Underactive, overactive, surgery?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. No surgery, I don't think. Just the pill. I was a kid when it started, pretty much.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Did anyone ever check your thyroid?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Once, yeah. They said the number was 7.2... no, wait, that's not it, they said borderline, something like 4-ish. I don't actually remember the number.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): And when was that test? I need you to repeat it, I clicked the wrong year box.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): 2019, or 2016, I really don't know which, so don't write a year down. They just called it borderline.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Are you on any thyroid medicine now? Say it again, I was fighting the mouse.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): No thyroid medicine. Just the vitamin D, two thousand units a day, and ibuprofen here and there for the knees.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): The knees, is that a real problem or once in a while?
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really often. Mostly after the stairs at the office. I don't know if it matters.
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me feel your neck. Chin up a little.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay, chin's up. Sorry, I talk when I'm nervous.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thyroid feels normal, I don't feel a goiter. Skin on your arms is a little dry, though.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Lotion's basically useless. Um, I need to walk something back.
[SEG0056] person_3 (DOCTOR): Go ahead. The order set is spinning, but I'm listening.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): My mood. I told you I was fine and I'm not — I've been really down, I cry in the car after work sometimes, and I don't enjoy TV or seeing friends anymore. I don't know, doctor. I still think it's the job and my age, but it's there.
[SEG0058] person_3 (DOCTOR): I appreciate you correcting that. Any thoughts of hurting yourself?
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. I just feel flat.
[SEG0060] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. Putting it together, the fatigue, the weight, the constipation, your mom's thyroid, I'm thinking possible hypothyroidism. I can't say that for certain today.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): So you're saying it's not just work?
[SEG0062] person_3 (DOCTOR): Work and age could still be in the mix. The low mood might be its own thing, too. That's on the differential, not a label I'm sticking on you.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. I don't know, doctor. I just want to stop dragging through the day.
[SEG0064] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll send labs. A TSH, a free T4, a CBC, and a basic metabolic panel.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Can that happen today? I've got a client call at two and I can't sit here all afternoon.
[SEG0066] person_3 (DOCTOR): The lab's down the hall, so it shouldn't eat your whole afternoon. We'll draw it today before you go. That's the plan, not a maybe.
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Are you starting me on a pill?
[SEG0068] person_3 (DOCTOR): No medicine from me until the results are back. Meanwhile, more water and some fiber for the constipation, and don't write the tiredness off as just getting older.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): Fiber, got it. My sister is obsessed with those gummy fibers. They taste like candy, which seems like cheating. Anyway.
[SEG0070] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come back in about three weeks and we'll go through the labs together. If you feel worse before then, call the office.
[SEG0071] person_1 (NURSE): I can walk you to the lab whenever you're set. Printer jammed on the instructions, so give me a second to reprint.

[SEG0073] person_1 (PATIENT): No, that's all. Thanks a lot.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr. Hale, come on through. I'll grab a blood pressure and a pulse before the doctor sees you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. I hope I have not kept anyone waiting.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Pressure is one forty-two over eighty-eight. Let me repeat that, you just sat down. One thirty-six over eighty-two. Pulse is seventy-eight.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I did come up the stairs rather quickly. The second reading is probably the fairer one.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): She's finishing a note, then she'll be right in.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mr. Hale, thanks for waiting. What can I do for you today?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): I have come about pain in my stomach, Doctor, and I have also been sleeping poorly. I felt it was time to have someone look at it.
[SEG0008] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'm Ruth. I live in with him, and I drove. Traffic on Maple was a mess, by the way, we circled the lot twice.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Glad you made it. Ruth, I'll want your view too. Mr. Hale, where is the pain, and what is it like?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): It is a burning pain in the upper part of my stomach, moderately uncomfortable. It comes most days, particularly after I eat, and a little purple pill takes the edge off.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long have you had it?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): About two weeks. Forgive me, that is not correct. It is closer to five weeks, though I cannot give you the exact date it began.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Most days for about five weeks, burning, after meals. Any vomiting with it?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have not vomited at all.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever, black stools, or chest pain?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever, no black stools, and no chest pain. I am quite certain of that.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Regarding the pill, I have been taking a little purple pill for heartburn, once a day. The dose is, um, maybe twenty milligrams. I am not certain of the number, and I never learned the proper name.
[SEG0018] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And he doesn't take it every morning. Some days I find it still sitting in the Monday slot on Wednesday.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): All right. A little purple heartburn pill, possibly twenty milligrams, once a day, not always actually swallowed, name unknown. We'll leave it described that way.
[SEG0020] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He's lost weight, too. His good trousers hang on him.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I must respectfully disagree. I do not believe I have lost any weight. It has been steady.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll hold both of those and not pretend we weighed him today. Tell me about the sleep.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): I lie awake a good deal, and the burning often wakes me. I would say the poor sleep has gone on for about two weeks.
[SEG0024] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Longer. It's been at least two months. He's in the kitchen at two in the morning, lights on, just standing there.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): So two weeks from you, Mr. Hale, and at least two months from Ruth. I'll call it somewhere between two weeks and two months, since you don't agree on a number.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): That is a fair summary. I simply had not counted the earlier nights.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking out loud here. Burning after meals, a heartburn pill that helps a little, this may be gastritis or acid reflux. I was going to suggest an over-the-counter antacid and skip blood tests. Before I settle on that, do you drink alcohol?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Only socially.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Socially covers a wide range. What does a usual evening look like?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, a bottle of wine most nights, perhaps. I did not mean to be evasive a moment ago.
[SEG0031] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Yeah. It's the bottle with dinner, not a splash in a glass. He corks it and it's gone.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): I appreciate you saying it straight. I'm not going to lecture you. A bottle most nights does change the plan I just sketched, because wine can inflame the stomach and it can stress the liver.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. Please tell me what you would advise.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me examine you first. Your abdomen is soft. There is mild tenderness in the upper middle, the epigastrium. No guarding and no rebound, and I can hear bowel sounds.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that spot is tender under your hand.
[SEG0036] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He flinched. I saw it.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): I had also been considering an ultrasound this afternoon. Soft belly, no fever, I'm setting that aside. My impression is gastritis or acid reflux, possibly stirred up by the wine. Not confirmed, just the best fit so far.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): An ultrasound did sound rather involved for a stomach ache.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Instead I'll order liver blood tests, a hepatic panel with the enzymes and bilirubin, because of the wine and this upper abdominal pain. For the pain I was going to start omeprazole at forty milligrams. Thinking it through, twenty milligrams is the better starting dose.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Would that be by mouth? And shall I keep taking the purple pill beside it?
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): By mouth, twenty milligrams every morning before breakfast, for the stomach pain. Leave the purple pill off while you are on the omeprazole, so we are not stacking two acid medicines.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Very well. I will set the purple one aside.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): If you can bring the wine down from a bottle toward a glass, or skip some nights, that will help both the stomach and the liver. No scolding in that, just how the organs work.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall try. The evenings are quiet, and the wine has become a habit I am not proud of. There is a biography on the nightstand I keep meaning to finish instead.
[SEG0045] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I can put the bottle in the cupboard instead of on the counter. That helps a little, sometimes.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back in two weeks to go over those blood results and see if the omeprazole is doing its job. If the pain turns severe, or you vomit blood, or your skin turns yellow, do not wait for that appointment. Go to the emergency room.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. You have explained it clearly, and I am grateful.

[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, one gets on with it, thank you. My husband has been marvellous, he's even taken up cooking.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has he? What's his signature dish?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Cheese on toast, I'm afraid. Burnt, mostly. But it's the thought that counts.

[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): There's some cramping low down, like period pains, mainly in the evenings.

[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Goodness, I really couldn't say. It might have been the week after, or perhaps before, it's all rather a blur.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's completely understandable. Anything else?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): I've been terribly tired, for about three weeks. I'm in bed by eight, which is not like me at all.

[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no fever at all. I did check, because the nurse at the ward told me to.

[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Only my appendix, taken out when I was fifteen. Nothing since.

[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): I felt dreadful for an hour or so, and the nurse made a note. Then everyone went rather vague about it.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): I see. So we have a possible allergy, no name, no clear reaction. I'll ask the hospital to send their notes, but let's be careful in the meantime.

[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Mostly old English roses. Tea scented, and a few climbers that have gone rather wild.

[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): That's very good to know, thank you. I may well do that.

[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I think you've covered everything. You've been very kind, doctor.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Look after yourself. The prescription will be at the front desk on your way out.
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): Marvellous. Goodbye, then.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Goodbye, and mind the step by the door.

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The Easter ham was separate. I overdid the ham, that's all.

[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Normal. Brown, once a day. No blood, no diarrhea.

[SEG0034] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And she still has two coffees every morning. That part is nonnegotiable.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): My daughter in Phoenix says switch to tea. I am not moving to Phoenix, it's an oven down there.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): Is it heartburn, a burn that climbs into the chest?

[SEG0038] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She stops talking and just holds her belly when it grabs her.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Like a what?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Like a fist, right under the breastbone. A six out of ten when it's going.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the sleep.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I wake up around two and the night is just over.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): When did that start?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I can't put a date on it. Maybe sometime in the winter. I really don't know, it crept up.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Have you lost weight?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, did you see that baking show, the one in the tent? Custard week, grown people crying over custard.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): I missed that one. The weight, though?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Pants fit the same. No weight loss.
[SEG0049] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Her appetite is off, though. She pushes the food around the plate.

[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you on?
