[SEG0056] person_4 (DOCTOR): What dose?
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten milligrams. No, scratch that, not ten, and not a hundred, that hundred was my sister's lab number. Twenty milligrams, once a day, by mouth, for the blood pressure.
[SEG0058] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She skips it some days. A couple of days a week, if she feels fine. I can't say she takes it the way it's written.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): I take it most days. You're fussing.
[SEG0060] person_4 (DOCTOR): So the prescription is twenty milligrams daily, and whether every dose gets taken is still a bit up in the air. Anything else?
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Advil, when my knees hurt. The two-hundred milligram tablets, two of them, a few times a week. Knees get stiff and achy.
[SEG0062] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And atorvastatin, forty milligrams every night, for her cholesterol.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): Right, forty, every night. My last doctor started that.
[SEG0064] person_4 (DOCTOR): So the high blood pressure and the high cholesterol are ongoing. Any surgeries in the past?
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Gallbladder came out about ten years ago. That's the only one.
[SEG0066] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any stomach problems in the family?
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother had ulcers. They had her drinking milk for it, which sounds silly now.
[SEG0068] person_4 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): My dad smoked cigars in the house. The drapes held the smell for years after he passed.
[SEG0070] person_4 (DOCTOR): I meant you.
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. Never. I hated the smell.
[SEG0072] person_4 (DOCTOR): What about alcohol?
[SEG0073] person_2 (PATIENT): Socially.
[SEG0074] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's a bottle of wine most nights.
[SEG0075] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, perhaps. Yes, a bottle, most nights, with dinner. It doesn't feel like a lot to me.
[SEG0076] person_4 (DOCTOR): Thank you, that's more useful than socially, and I'm not going to scold you. A bottle most nights can irritate the stomach and the liver, so I do want to check the liver.
[SEG0077] person_2 (PATIENT): If the next sentence is give up coffee, we are going to have words.
[SEG0078] person_4 (DOCTOR): No words, and I'm not making you quit coffee cold. Let me examine your belly.
[SEG0079] person_4 (DOCTOR): Abdomen is soft. It's tender when I press in the epigastrium, under the breastbone. No guarding and no rebound tenderness.
[SEG0080] person_2 (PATIENT): Ow, yes, that's the spot. And, well, actually, mornings I am queasy. Sick to my stomach until I eat a cracker. I told you I wasn't, but I am.
[SEG0081] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you came back to that. Thinking out loud, pain after meals, wine most nights, queasy in the morning, no vomiting, this fits gastritis best. I can't rule out an ulcer.
[SEG0082] person_2 (PATIENT): An ulcer sounds like my mother. I don't love that.
[SEG0083] person_4 (DOCTOR): It's on the list, not a settled diagnosis. I'm going to start omeprazole, forty, no, twenty milligrams is the better start, by mouth every morning, thirty minutes before breakfast, for the stomach pain.
[SEG0084] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll also order liver blood tests, a hepatic panel, because of the wine and the pain. The lab can draw them today after we finish.
[SEG0085] person_2 (PATIENT): Needles. All right, I guess.
[SEG0086] person_4 (DOCTOR): Please stop the Advil while the stomach is irritated, it can make this worse. Ease off the spicy and greasy food, and try cutting the wine back. For sleep, no coffee after lunch, and keep a regular bedtime. If the pain turns severe, or you vomit blood, or you pass black stool, go to the ER.
[SEG0087] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll put the Advil up high. The wine is going to be the argument.
[SEG0088] person_4 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks. We'll look at the liver tests and see if the omeprazole is helping. The front desk can book it.
[SEG0089] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. If that beagle is quiet, maybe I'll have slept.
[SEG0090] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll take the sleep as it comes. See you in two weeks.

[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, give me more detail on it, whatever comes to mind.

[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had more breathless than usual before, or is this the first time?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, a bit, last winter. It settled by itself back then.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): What operations have you had, if any?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): So, yes, I had my appendix taken out, when I was in my twenties.

[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm vegetarian and have been for years.

[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): What conditions have you been treated for in the past?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): I've had COPD for five years now.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, COPD is known to us, good to have that clear.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me ask about allergies, anything at all?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I've never reacted to anything.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): A few quick ones: chest pain, fever or coughing up blood?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): No chest pain, fever or coughing up blood, none of it.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has there been any swollen ankles?

[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, may I examine you now?

[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): You can sit up now.

[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): A sputum sample is what I'd like next, for purulent sputum.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): When would that take place?

[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, alright.

[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have a good day.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, have a seat. What can I do for you today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Honestly, it's hardly anything. I nearly didn't come. The knee's been a bit off, that's all.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, tell me how it's been for you.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Right knee. Going down the stairs it grumbles, and at night if I turn over it wakes me sometimes. Months, maybe since the spring, I couldn't tell you exactly. Not every day, and I still get about fine.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it stop you doing things, or are you mostly carrying on?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Carrying on. I'm not an invalid. Stairs are just annoying, that's it.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any swelling you've spotted, or does the knee give way under you?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling. And it doesn't give way. I'm not keeling over.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it lock, get stuck at all?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): What have you tried for it so far?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): That gel from the chemist. Diclofenac. I rub a bit on the knee.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Twice a day. Morning and when I get into bed. Takes the edge off, I suppose. Not a miracle.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any tablets as well, or just the gel?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes the, um, naproxen— no, I don't take naproxen. Ibuprofen, from the pharmacy, if it's a bad day. I'm not one for pills.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you know the strength, and how many you take?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Two hundred milligram ones. One or two, with a bit of food. Maybe two or three times in a week. Not regularly.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your stomach, with those? Any pain, sickness, that sort of thing?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Stomach's completely fine. No trouble at all.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. Has your weight shifted at all lately? Knees notice that, sometimes.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit, yeah. Half a stone, maybe, since Christmas. People go on about it. I'm not huge.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you managing any walks, or has that dropped off?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): I walk to the paper shop and back. That's plenty. Gyms are not for me.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mind if I have a look and a feel of the knee?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Go on, then. You'll see it's nothing.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): There's tenderness along the inside of the right knee, and a little crunching as I bend it. No swelling that I can feel.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): There you are. I said it wasn't swollen.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did you see any of the cricket over the weekend? Absolute chaos at the end.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Had the radio on while I was peeling potatoes. England were all over the shop. Typical.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): My grandson was yelling at the telly. Eight years old and he's already picking the team.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Ha. Mine's mad for football. They came round Sunday and the ball ended up in the flower bed twice.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): The weather didn't help, pouring from lunchtime. I sat in traffic on the ring road forty minutes just for a pint of milk.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Those roadworks by the big supermarket. Been there since March. You'd think they'd finished by now.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): I know. Anyway, sorry, back to you, if that's alright.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, one thing. I said the stomach was fine. Well, I do get a bit of heartburn after the ibuprofen. Not every time. It's minor, not proper pain. Hardly worth mentioning.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you said. Keep the ibuprofen just for the odd bad day, and if that heartburn gets worse, leave the tablets off. The gel is easier on the stomach.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): The gel's fine. I'll carry on with that. The tablets are only now and then anyway.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): From what you've told me, and from examining it, I think this is most likely wear and tear, osteoarthritis in the right knee. That's my working impression, not a definite diagnosis.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Wear and tear. I'm seventy-four. Course it is. Everyone my age has something.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): We might refer you to physiotherapy, or later on we could think about an injection into the knee, but I don't want us to decide either of those today.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't fancy a needle, thanks. And physio sounds like a lot of faff for a niggle.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's fair. We'll leave both for now.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Good.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): We might do an x-ray if it hasn't settled. Otherwise I won't put you through it yet.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't need a scan. It'll sort itself.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's see you in two weeks, and we'll take another look then.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, alright. I'll be fine, you'll see. Probably a waste of your time.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): So, um, I had the ultrasound last month, and the report said something about my liver. I wasn't sure what to...
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, take your time. Let's start with what the report said. Do you have it with you?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Right here. It says, uh, fatty liver. Mild. And I've been kind of freaking out since.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): I understand. Fat in the liver is quite common, and mild is the reassuring word there. Your family doctor sent you to talk through your medicines, right?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. She said the liver can be affected by, you know, tablets. So I brought the list.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good thinking. We'll go through each. First, how have you been feeling? Any symptoms?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Not much. Some mild discomfort on my right side, under the ribs. Sometimes. It's, um, more of a nagging than a pain.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): A nagging discomfort under the right ribs. How often?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): A couple of times a week? After big meals, I guess. I haven't really...
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's okay. You haven't noticed it anywhere else?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Just there.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you noticed your eyes or skin looking yellow?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no yellow. My wife would have said something, she notices everything.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Now the medicines. What's the first one on your list?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Metformin. 500 mg, twice a day, with meals. For my diabetes.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Metformin, 500 mg twice a day, for the diabetes. Which type of diabetes?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Type 2. Diagnosed about six years ago.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks. Next?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Atorvastatin. 20 mg, at bedtime. It's for, uh, cholesterol. I've had high cholesterol for a long time.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Atorvastatin, 20 mg at bedtime, for your cholesterol. Any muscle aches with that?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't think so. Hmm, maybe my calves sometimes, but I don't know if that's the...
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll keep an eye on that. What else?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Lisinopril, 10 mg. Once a day, in the morning. For blood pressure.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lisinopril, 10 mg once a day for blood pressure. Is that all?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, and the baby aspirin. 81 mg. My cardiologist, um, a few years ago... Anyway, I take it every morning too.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Aspirin, 81 mg every morning. So four medicines in total. Anything over the counter? Supplements?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing else. I'm kind of scared to take anything extra now, because of the liver.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's sensible. Just check with us or the pharmacist before you add anything new.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, I will.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is there anything in the family I should know about? Liver trouble, or other illness?
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): My father had diabetes too. He had it for a long time.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, thank you. Let me have a quick feel of your tummy.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your abdomen is soft, and I can't feel anything unusual under the ribs on the right.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): That's a relief. I was afraid you'd find a lump or something.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not at all. Let me also read your numbers. Blood pressure is 134 over 82, and weight is 94 kilograms.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): The weight's gone up a little. I know. I'm, um...
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): It happens. Let me say back what I'm hearing. Mild fatty liver on the scan, a nagging right-sided discomfort now and then, and four regular medicines.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, that's it.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Those four medicines are all well-established, and none is a common cause of fatty liver. I'd like to order liver blood tests to see how your liver is working.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. Like, regular blood work?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, a simple blood draw. You can do it at the lab on your way out.
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): And what should I do about the fat? Is there a pill for it?
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not really. Gradual weight loss, regular movement, and cutting back on sugary drinks help the most. Even a small loss makes a difference.
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): I can try that. I just... I'm not sure where to start.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Start small. Swap one sugary drink a day for water, and add a ten-minute walk after dinner.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. Water and a walk. I can do that.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Exactly. I'd like to see you again in three months, so we can look at the blood results and how things are going.
[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): Three months. Okay. Thank you. I feel a lot calmer now.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): You did well to come in, and bring the list. See you then.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll grab your obs before Dr Lang comes in. Blood pressure's one twenty-eight over seventy-eight, heart rate's one hundred and eight, oxygen sat ninety-eight percent.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): A hundred and eight? Is that dangerous? I can feel it in my throat just sitting here.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): It's on the quick side, but I'm not the one to unpack it. She'll be in in a tick.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hi, I'm Dr Lang. Racing heart, is that what's brought you in?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, and I get really puffed, like I can't finish a sentence. It's worse at night in bed, and it also kicks off before exams or if I've got a meeting at work. But I don't think it's stress. I'm not a stressy person.
[SEG0006] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'm his partner, I live with him. It's been three months, easy, since the start of autumn. He bolts upright at night with it.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): It is not three months. It's six weeks, maybe a bit over. And I don't bolt upright every night, just some nights.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): So you two don't quite line up on the timing. I'll park it as weeks to a few months. With the racing, any dizziness? Any chest pain?
[SEG0009] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He goes pale and dizzy. I've watched him grab the bench and sit down.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not get dizzy. There's no chest pain. It's just this thumping. She's worrying more than I am.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): The breathlessness — with the thumping, or on its own? And when did the puffing actually start?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): With it. I can't get a proper breath in, worse lying down at night. Before meetings too, but that's a stuffy room, not... you know. The start, I can't put a date on it, it just crept up.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): How much coffee are you putting away?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I ask something first? Could this actually be my heart packing up? I'm only twenty-four, but my uncle—
[SEG0015] person_4 (CAREGIVER): His uncle had a heart attack at sixty. Totally different thing. Tell her about the coffee.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, sorry. Six or seven long blacks a day, and most arvos a couple of those big V cans. Sometimes three if I'm cramming.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you vape, or smoke cigarettes?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Vape. Nicotine, the twenty milligram pods, pretty much all day. I was going to quit before the exams but—
[SEG0019] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He gets through a pod every day and a half. And he reckons he's fine, but he's awake revising till two. He doesn't sleep.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I sleep. Well, not properly — the heart thing wakes me, that's all. I am not anxious. Can we not make this a stress thing?
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any tablets just now, prescribed or from the chemist?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I tried something a couple of weeks back for the racing, little brown bottle, white tablets. Never clocked the name. Maybe two a day? Stopped last week, they did nothing.
[SEG0023] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I thought they were magnesium.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): They weren't, I don't think. I honestly couldn't tell you what was in them.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. I had amoxicillin last year for a sore throat and I was completely fine.
[SEG0027] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Your mum always said you came up in a swelling with penicillin when you were little.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): That story's ancient and I don't buy it. If the amoxicillin was fine, I'm not allergic.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any operations? Previous heart trouble?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No operations. Heart was fine until this started.
[SEG0031] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Sorry we were twenty minutes late, by the way. Parramatta Road was banked up forever.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): That rain this morning didn't help. I got soaked just crossing from the car park.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): We had the cricket on the radio the whole way. Sheffield Shield, Smith was set, and then they stopped for the rain.
[SEG0034] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And that nick they didn't even review. He'll be filthy.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah I was yelling at the radio like an idiot. Anyway.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): I only caught the highlights. Righto, back to you. Let me have a listen.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pulse is regular, just fast. Heart sounds are normal. Lungs are clear, no wheeze. No swelling at the ankles.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any weight change, feeling unusually hot, or shaky hands? I'm asking with the thyroid in mind.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): I've dropped a bit of weight, but I've been skipping lunch, so that might be why. I do feel hot at night when it happens. Hands aren't shaky. Is a bit of weight loss a bad sign, and how much is too much?
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Without a number I can't call it good or bad. Skipping lunch muddies it, so I won't hang a story on the weight.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): So what do you actually think this is? Am I going to collapse before the exam? Do I have to stop coffee completely? And does an ECG hurt?
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to tell you you're about to collapse. Thinking it through, the coffee, the energy drinks and the vaping can all drive a fast heart and that air hunger, an overactive thyroid can look just the same, and I can't rule out a rhythm problem until we've got a tracing. I am not labelling this anxiety. The timing around exams is a flag, not a diagnosis.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): If the thyroid's normal and the ECG's normal, then what? Do I just live like this? Can I keep vaping if I cut the coffee? What if I faint — I haven't fainted, I'm just asking.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): If those come back normal and the episodes are still happening, we might organise a Holter, a recorder you wear for a day or so. Not ordering that today — let's see what the tests say. I'd like you to wind the coffee and the Vs right down, and have a real go at stopping the vape. I'll also show you a slow breathing exercise for when it starts at night — in for four, out for six, a few minutes.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Is the breathing instead of coming back? When do I come back? And who rings me if something's wrong on the bloods?
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Breathing is for the episodes, not instead of review. Come back in a fortnight either way and we'll go through it together; we'll contact you sooner if something on the tests needs it. I'll order an ECG today, plus thyroid bloods, a TSH and a free T4. If you faint, or you get heavy chest pain, don't wait for the fortnight, go to emergency.
[SEG0047] person_1 (NURSE): I'll walk you down for the ECG, and the blood form will be at the desk. Won't take long.

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Three months, roughly. Since we got a new manager who likes everyone to speak up. I just find a reason to be somewhere else.

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): My stomach drops, and I start rehearsing what I'd say, over and over. Then it feels easier just to skip it. Which is awful, isn't it?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Sertraline, 100 milligrams once a day, in the morning. And the omeprazole, 20 milligrams, also every morning. Then propranolol, 10 milligrams, only when I've got a presentation.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sertraline, omeprazole and propranolol as needed, thank you for being so clear. Any problems taking them, any side effects that bother you?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing really. I just worry about being on them for so long. Is it normal to still need them after this long?
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Many people stay on sertraline for a good while, and it's doing a job for you. I've got in your notes social anxiety, reflux and eczema. Is that all still accurate?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that's all of it. Though the eczema is mostly quiet now, just my hands in winter.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): And any operations in the past, anything at all?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Only my tonsils, when I was nine. I don't remember much, just the ice cream afterwards.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's the best part, of course. Now I need to ask about some darker thoughts, which I ask everybody. Any thoughts of harming yourself?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no. Never like that. It's more that I feel stupid and ashamed, not that I want to... no.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you told me, and feeling ashamed is something we can work on together. And when your heart does race, any chest pain or fainting?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no chest pain and no fainting. It's only that nervous thumping, and then it passes. Is that normal?
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's a common pattern, and it's reassuring that there's no pain. Now a few quick questions about the rest of your body. Any problems with your breathing?

[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulse is 84 and regular. Temperature is 36.5 degrees. Oxygen saturation is 99 percent.

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): That's a relief. I thought they'd be shaking.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): They're not. Now, I'd like to arrange a blood test, to check your thyroid and blood count. Anxiety can sometimes be mimicked or worsened by those.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Do you think something's wrong with my thyroid? Is that why I'm like this?

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): All right. Is that painful? I hate needles.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): The ECG is just stickers on your chest, and the blood test takes seconds. The receptionist will give you the forms on your way out.

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll try. I don't know if I can do the wine thing every night, doctor.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Trying is enough for now. I'll see you back in about two weeks, when those labs are in. If the pain turns sharp, or you vomit blood, don't wait on me, go to the emergency room.

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, thank you. That is the one. I took this morning's dose.

[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): None. My brother has confused me with our cousin. She had the penicillin trouble as a child. I did not.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Prior reaction to amoxicillin? Hives, wheeze?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): Looking now. Scattered pink welts on the forearms and chest, plus scratch marks.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hands are dry. No welts on the palms. Throat is clear. No swelling of the lips.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): I am embarrassed about the scratch marks. I did try not to scratch.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Skin doesn't look infected. I am not naming a single cause. This could be the amoxicillin, the cream, or the shrimp. I cannot tell them apart today.

[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Understood. I will not take that one.
[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the rash is not settling in one week, come back. We would arrange patch testing then, not today.

[SEG0059] person_3 (DOCTOR): If your lips swell or you cannot breathe, go to the emergency room. Otherwise stay on the water tablet, start the cetirizine, and stop those two new products.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. You have been very clear.
[SEG0061] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll send the cetirizine to your pharmacy on file. You're all set at the desk.

[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): White coat. Have you actually measured it at home?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): My brother's machine, once or twice. I do not remember the figures. Not this high, that I am sure of.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That machine is the brother's, doctor. He does not use it regular. I have not seen a proper reading.

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No giddiness. Clear no.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Are you on any blood pressure tablets?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No BP tablets. I take only the vitamin, and for the knee some Crocin from the pharmacy when it aches.

[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): So paracetamol five hundred at night, only if needed. Any allergy to medicines, or anything else?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): No allergies. I can eat and take whatever.

[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): No sugar, no heart problem. My father had a stroke, I remembered just now, he was seventy-something, but that is his story. My daughter in Pune keeps forwarding health messages, full tension.
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Father had a stroke, noted. You yourself, any stroke, any surgery?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): No stroke for me. No operation ever. Not even appendix.
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Smoking? Alcohol?
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): I left smoking ten years back. No alcohol. Tea I take a lot, that is the only habit, morning to night.
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): Okay. I am not starting any BP tablet today. Both readings are high, the second a bit lower, and the home values we simply have not seen.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): No new tablet, good. I was worried you would start one immediately.

[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks is fine, after the society meeting. And kindly the gym form? They are chasing me.
[SEG0059] person_4 (DOCTOR): The gym form I will not sign until we see those home readings. If the knee is still the same then, we can talk about the scan. Bring the diary, both of you.

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None at all.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any operations? Diabetes, or anything else I should have on the list?

[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll have a quick feel, if you lie back. Knees bent, that's it.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Go on, then. It won't even hurt, watch.

[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you for putting it plainly. I'm not going to have a go. A bottle most nights is more than an odd glass, and it can inflame the stomach and chop up your sleep, so it does change what I want to do.

[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, leave the Rennies off while you're taking the omeprazole. No need for both. And if you can ease the wine down, even towards half a bottle, the pain and the waking have a better chance of settling. That's practical, not a telling-off.

[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Maybe it is, and maybe it isn't. Two weeks, with the results. First tablet tomorrow morning.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Tomorrow. Alright. Cheers, then.

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): About eight to ten? The last period was around Diwali, or after. I can't pin the day. We had family over, there was so much food, my auntie made that carrot halwa, I ate way too much, totally off topic, sorry.

[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. It's just a bit of brown when I wipe.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is the pain more on one side?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose, sometimes, not really. It sort of moves around.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any shoulder pain, or dizziness?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No shoulder pain. I went a bit woozy in the shower yesterday but it passed, I just stood up too quick. My sister's like that, she's anaemic, forever telling me to eat spinach.

[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No, gone.

[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in, grab a seat. Sorry about the wait — we've been flat out this arvo.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): That's alright. Um, I don't know, doctor, I feel a bit silly coming in. I've just been so tired.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not silly. How long's it been?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Months. Six months? Maybe longer, I can't pin the start. I figured it was work — I'm a project manager, desk all day, deadlines are brutal. And I'm fifty-two, so maybe it's just age.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Could be either. Is it that you can't get going, or you're wrecked after the day?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Both, sort of. I sleep heaps, nine hours easy, and I still wake up tired. It's not that I can't get to sleep.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Feeling cold as well?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. I blamed the office aircon. Well, actually it's at home too, even with the doona on. A few months.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any change in your weight?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think I've put on that much.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are your clothes fitting the same?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, no. Jeans are two sizes up, so yes I have. Five or six kilos. I don't know exactly — I gave up on the scales.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about the bowels?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Constipated, honestly. Maybe three times a week, and it used to be every morning. No blood in the stool.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pain with that?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No pain really. Just slow, hard to get going. Sorry, that's grim.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): How's your mood sitting in all this?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Flat. I don't enjoy the footy or dinner with my sister like I did. I pinned it on work being hectic. I don't know if I'm depressed, doctor.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you taken anything for the bowels, or for your mood?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Coloxyl, from the chemist. One tablet a day for about a week, then I stopped because it didn't do much. Nothing for mood. I never have.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me think out loud. Tired, cold, weight up, sluggish bowels, low mood — that pattern can be an underactive thyroid. Any thyroid disease in the family?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Mum had it. Underactive, I think. She was on tablets for years. She died a few years back, so I don't know the fine detail.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): And has your own thyroid been checked?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Years ago, yeah. The old GP did a blood test and they said it was borderline. I never followed it up. I don't know the number, and I couldn't say when it was.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, so we've got 'borderline' as you remember it, not a number I can rely on. Has anyone ever actually diagnosed you with a thyroid condition?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never. I'm pretty well apart from this. Oh, random one — I reckon the parking meter's about to run out.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll keep it moving. Any chest pain, or shortness of breath when you walk?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about your skin and hair?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Skin's a bit dry. Hair, I don't know, doctor. Maybe there's more in the brush. I'm not sure, so I wouldn't trust that.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll put down the dry skin and leave the hair. On examination the thyroid isn't enlarged, there's no lump, the heart sounds are fine, and your ankles aren't swollen.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): So is this just age? I don't know, doctor. I had a coffee on the way, if you're doing bloods — do I need to fast?
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): No need to fast, the coffee's fine. I'm not calling it hypothyroidism today. The working idea is an underactive thyroid, given the symptoms and your mum, but burning out at work stays on the list. I won't start thyroxine on a guess.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. I just want to feel like myself again.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll order a thyroid function test and a full blood count today. If those thyroid numbers are out of whack and this hasn't settled, we might do an ultrasound of the thyroid — I am not booking that now.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): And the, um, not going to the toilet. Anything I should do meanwhile?
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep your fluids up and add some fibre, pears or oats. If your mood drops hard, or you can't get out of bed, come back sooner or ring the clinic, don't sit on it. Otherwise let's see you in a couple of weeks once the results are in — reception can book that as you leave.

[SEG0016] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I've tried to think as well. I can't put a month on it either.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, we'll leave the start date open. Coffee, energy drinks, how much in a day?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Well, four cups, maybe five. And a Monster if there's a deadline. It's not hectic.
[SEG0019] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's a Monster in the car and another at her desk, and the vape is in her hand the whole time.

[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): No, I don't take medicine, nothing regular and nothing occasional.

[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): No allergies. Never had one.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Asthma, a thyroid problem, any heart condition you've been told about?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): No, none of that. I've always just cracked on.
[SEG0027] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry, random, but the N1 was a proper mess this morning. We sat through three cycles at that robot by Canal Walk.
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): And then he wanted to talk about the Proteas the whole way. Did you see that catch at the boundary? The third umpire bottled it completely.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ja, I saw the highlights with my coffee. That lbw was a shocker. Wind was mad yesterday as well, dust everywhere.
[SEG0030] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): My brother's little boy tried to fly a kite in it. Thing went straight over the neighbour's wall and we spent ages fetching it out of a lemon tree.
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): He's four and already shouting at the TV umpire. Lekker attitude. Anyway, sorry, we got sidetracked.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sharp, no problem. Let me examine you, then Sister can read me those numbers.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lungs are clear both sides, no wheeze. Heart sounds are normal, no murmur. Pulse is regular, just a bit quick. Ankles aren't swollen.

[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): So I'm thinking out loud. The flutter and the puffing, clustered at night and before you have to perform, plus that much caffeine and the vape, that package often is the stimulant load. I still don't want to miss an overactive thyroid or a rhythm problem.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): So you think it's just the coffee. I can live with that. I don't need a whole workup.

[SEG0041] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll hide the Monsters. She won't.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): Ag, I'll try. I'm not promising I'll become a herbal tea person.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks and we'll go through the ECG and the bloods. If you get actual chest pain, or you faint, don't wait, come straight in or to casualty.
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): Two weeks is fine. It won't be anything.
[SEG0045] person_1 (NURSE): Sharp, I'll walk you to the ECG after this. Lab forms I'll print just now.

[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, is this radiator doing anything? It's either freezing or roasting in here.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm alright. I'll keep the jacket on. Always do.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): That flat, can't-be-bothered feeling — most days?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Most days. Months of it. I don't make a performance out of it.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): I need to ask this gently. Any thoughts of not wanting to be here, or of hurting yourself?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Definitely not. Never crossed my mind. I'm not about to do anything daft.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you, that's clear. How's eating?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I eat enough. Well, not much, actually. She says the trousers are hanging off, but I haven't been near the scales, so don't go writing a weight down.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): No number, then. Leaving fine aside, what word fits the mood?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Low. Empty. Bored of the whole lot. I don't cry, nothing like that.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any panic, or winding yourself up?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'm not anxious. Switched off, that's all.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): And concentrating — the telly, or when your wife talks?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Telly's a blur, couldn't tell you the plot. I drift off mid-sentence. That's the bit that's newer.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you drink?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Couple of beers most nights. A bit more since the job went. No spirits. Supposed to take the edge off.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): And smoking?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Filthy habit.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any regular medicines?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): The water tablet. Little white one, every morning, for my blood pressure. Don't ask me the name, it won't come.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything from the chemist for the nights?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Nytol, the blue box, one at night when I remember, maybe three times a week. I skip it if I've had the beers. Waste of money, really.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): So you're not sure you're using it the way it's meant to be used.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. I just take one if I think of it. Could be doing it all wrong.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Were you ever put on something for your mood?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Sertraline, years ago, after my dad died. I stopped it. Head went woolly. Totally different thing.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): What dose was that, if you remember?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifty milligrams, I think — might have been a hundred — no, fifty, I'm pretty sure. Once a day.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): You came off it yourself?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. After a few months I felt alright, so I didn't bother you lot again.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cuff on for a second. Sorry, it's cold.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Go on. It'll be normal. Always is.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hundred and thirty-eight over eighty-six. Pulse seventy-two. Nothing worrying there.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): This is a working impression, not a finished diagnosis. It looks like a depressive episode — low mood, poor sleep, loss of interest — tied up with the redundancy.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): You can call it that. I still say I'm mostly fine.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): I don't want to start a tablet today. If things haven't shifted in four weeks, sertraline would be the one I'd consider, but come back in four weeks either way.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks. She'll be thrilled I showed up.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Between now and then, ease off the beers on weeknights, pick a bedtime and stick to it, and skip the Nytol if you've been drinking. If thoughts of hurting yourself ever do turn up, ring the surgery the same day or call one one one, don't wait for me.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on through. I'll grab your obs while he's still stuck on the phone. Jacket can stay on.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ta. Sorry, the Monash was a car park. I nearly turned around and went back to the office.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): It's been like that all morning. Blood pressure's one thirty-two over seventy-eight, pulse is fifty-eight, and the scales say eighty-six point four kilos.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Eighty-six? I was under eighty last time I bothered. Couldn't tell you when. I'm not fussed, honestly.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put that in the chart. There's water on the bench if you want it. He won't be long.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, sorry. This thing's been spinning since nine. What's brought you in, then?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Probably nothing. I've been a bit tired. Work's flat out and I'm fifty-two, so I reckon that's the whole story.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tired like you could sleep, or tired like there's no petrol in the tank?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): No petrol. I still get through the day. I'm not dropping off in meetings or anything dramatic.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long's that been?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, months. Since last winter. Well, actually, it might've been the winter before. I can't keep the years straight.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hang on, I've clicked the wrong patient. Say the timing again?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know the date. Last winter, or the one before. A good few months. It's been much the same, so I left it.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): And you're putting the whole thing on work.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Work and being fifty-two, yeah. I do the accounts at Knox council. Late ones most nights. Anyone would be wiped.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Knox, right. Are you feeling the cold, or is it just this room?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): This room's fine. I am a bit cold, even at home with the heater going. I blamed the office aircon for ages, but it's not only there. Still, it's nothing.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, a box just popped up over your notes. Cold at home, did you say?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Heater on, and I still feel it. It's mild. I'm not wrapped in a doona or anything.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): The nurse has you at eighty-six point four. Have you actually put weight on?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit, yeah. I was under eighty whenever I last stood on a scale, a couple of years back or longer, and I never wrote it down. Desk job and biscuits in the tearoom. Hardly an illness.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): What are the bowels doing?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit sluggish. Every second day, and sometimes I skip two. I wasn't even going to mention it.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the bowl, or black stools?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No blood. They're just slow. I eat fine, before you ask.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mood. Are you flat, or is this only the energy?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm a bit flat, if you want it straight. Not depressed, not crying in the car. Just over the job and getting older. I still front up.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. Flat, and you reckon it's the job. Any thyroid problems in the family, while this page thinks about loading?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Mum had an underactive thyroid, little tablets for years. She's gone now, so I can't ask her the name of them. Don't make a big thing of it, she was old.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Did anyone ever check yours?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Once, yeah. They said it was borderline. I was meant to repeat it and I didn't, because I felt fine.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Borderline. Was there a number, a TSH, anything?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No number that I remember. Just borderline, they said, and the letter's long gone. Last winter, or the winter before. Same muddle as the tiredness.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm in the results tab and I can't see a thyroid test on this file at all. Somewhere else?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Might've been the bulk-billing clinic in Bayswater. Or before I started coming here. I didn't keep it. They weren't worried, so I wasn't.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Righto. And it's frozen again. Of course. Did that Monash mess get you the whole way in?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Stopped dead back to the Springvale exit. A ute into the barrier, everyone slowing down for a stickybeak.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): I thought I was clever coming Burwood Road. Still took forty minutes from Box Hill. Should've been fifteen.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): At least the sun's out. Had the cricket on the radio. They're getting flogged, can't bat to save themselves.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): I stayed up for the first session like a dill. Slips dropped three catches. There goes the weekend and it's only Tuesday.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): My brother-in-law texted a rant about the selectors before I'd had a coffee. I didn't even reply. Whole summer down the drain if this keeps up.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yeah, don't get me started. Alright, cursor's back. Your hair. Is it coming out in the shower more than it used to?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Same as ever. Thin on top since my thirties, nothing new. I'm not shedding.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chin up a bit, I'll feel your neck. Still half an eye on this login, sorry.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Go on, then. You'll say my hands are cold. I already told you.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): No goitre. The thyroid isn't enlarged. Hands are cool, yeah, but nothing dramatic on a quick feel.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): So that's it? I've got to be back before one.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not quite. Cold, tired, weight up, slow bowels, and your mum had an underactive thyroid. This could be an underactive thyroid, a working idea, not a label. It might still just be the job and your age, and I can't split them from here.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): If you say so. Feels like a lot of fuss for being a bit off.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll do a blood test, thyroid function. I want an actual number, not a memory of someone saying borderline. Pathology downstairs can take it today if you've got ten minutes.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): I've got something at two. If it's quick, I'll do it today. I don't want another bit of paper living in the car.
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): It's quick. I'll add a full blood count on the same form, only because we're already taking blood. Not because I've thought of some other disease.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. And I'm not going on some mad diet, if that's the next speech.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): Don't. No crash diet, and don't buy thyroid tablets or kelp from the chemist while we wait. Come back in two weeks and we'll go through whatever comes back.
[SEG0055] person_1 (NURSE): I'll print the form and walk you down if you like. Two tubes and you're done.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hey, Mr. Ellison, come on in and have a seat. What got you in today?

[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did the cough actually start?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I almost said two weeks, but that's wrong. The cold was three weeks ago, and the dry cough started with it, so three weeks. I lose track because the days all feel the same when you're hacking.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the cold itself, is any of that still going?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Runny nose, scratchy throat, that stuff lasted a few days and then it quit. Nose is fine now, throat doesn't hurt. The cough is the only thing that stuck around, which is why I blamed the cold and waited.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is it there all day, or more at certain times?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): All day, but nights are worse, right in the throat. Lying down sets it off, and if I talk a lot, like I'm doing right now, it bubbles up. Sipping water calms the tickle for a minute and then it's back. I moved to the guest room so my wife can sleep, which she appreciates and also does not.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever with this? Shortness of breath?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. I checked with the old thermometer twice and I wasn't hot. I'm not short of breath either. I walk the dog around the block every morning and I can do that fine, it's just embarrassing when I cough the whole way.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain at all? Any wheezing?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. And I don't wheeze, it's not that tight whistling thing, it's just a dry hack. I started to go off on a whole story about the dog and, um, I'll spare you.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you coughing anything up, mucus or blood?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing at all. Dry as a bone. I tried honey in tea because my neighbor, not a doctor, swears by it, and it tasted fine and did basically nothing. Sorry, that's a tangent.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): No problem. You're followed for blood pressure. Tell me what you're actually taking these days.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): High blood pressure for, um, five-ish years, maybe a bit more, I never remember the exact anniversary. The water pill is hydrochlorothiazide. I always want to say twelve and a half milligrams, but I looked, it's twenty-five milligrams, once every morning, and I've been on that one for years.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): And then two weeks ago we added ramipril. I had it in my head that it was twenty milligrams, but the bottle this morning says ten milligrams, once a day. Both of them by mouth, with breakfast, every day. I don't skip.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me say that back. Hydrochlorothiazide twenty-five milligrams each morning for years, ramipril ten milligrams each morning for the last two weeks, both by mouth. That's the list?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the whole list. No vitamins, no aspirin, I know everybody my age is on aspirin but I'm not. And I blamed the cold for the cough, not the new pill.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): What made you think it wasn't the ramipril?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): My brother Dave has high blood pressure too, and he's on lisinopril, I think twenty milligrams, and he has never coughed from it. So I figured if he can take an ACE inhibitor, mine shouldn't be the problem. His pill, not mine, I just mean the comparison.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Got it, his lisinopril stays his. We'll come back to the timing. Any medicine allergies, or food, anything like that?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. Penicillin is fine, aspirin is fine, I've never swollen up or gotten a rash from a drug. I feel like I should have a more interesting answer and I don't.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): So no known allergies. Do you smoke?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Never have. My dad did and the house smelled like an ashtray, so I never started. I'll have a beer on Sundays watching the game, that's the alcohol story, very boring. I still work part-time at the hardware store, mostly the garden section.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any surgeries in the past?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Appendix out when I was twenty-two. Emergency, middle of the night, very dramatic at the time and completely irrelevant now. Nothing since.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. I'm going to check your pressure and listen to your chest. Give me a second.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Sure. The cuff always squeezes more than I expect. I tell myself that every visit and it still surprises me.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure is one thirty-eight over eighty-six. Heart rate seventy-four. Oxygen sat ninety-eight percent.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Office number looks decent. At home it's been up in the one-fifties, which is the whole reason we added the ramipril. I keep a notebook, very analog, my wife wants me to use an app.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lungs are clear, I don't hear any wheeze, your throat looks normal, and there's no swelling in the legs.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay, good. I was half convinced you'd find something rattling around in there. The cough feels so loud from the inside.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me pull the story together before I say what I think. Dry cough for three weeks, started with a cold, runny nose and scratchy throat gone after a few days, worse at night and lying down, water helps only briefly.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. And no fever, no phlegm, no chest pain, I can breathe fine.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the medicines: water pill twenty-five milligrams for years, ramipril ten milligrams started two weeks ago, so the cough actually began about a week before the ramipril.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Huh. I hadn't lined it up like that. I was so stuck on the cold idea that I didn't count the days against the pill. That's a little annoying, that I missed it.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to call this a definite drug cough. It could be the ramipril, those can cause a dry cough in some people, and it could also just be the tail of the cold, since it started first and your exam is clear.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): So you're saying it might be either, and you don't know yet.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's exactly it. I can't say for sure today which one it is. What I do want to do is stop the ramipril and switch you to losartan, fifty milligrams once a day.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Losartan. Is that still for the blood pressure? And fifty milligrams, not twenty-five? I mix numbers up, I want to hear it twice.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, for the blood pressure. Fifty milligrams, once each morning, by mouth. Keep the hydrochlorothiazide at twenty-five. Don't take any more ramipril, starting now.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Stop ramipril today, start losartan tomorrow morning with the water pill. I won't borrow my brother's lisinopril, that was never the plan, I was only talking.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. If your lips or tongue swell, or your chest gets tight, that needs the emergency room, don't wait for me.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Lips, tongue, tight chest, ER. Got it. What about the cough itself, do I take something for it, like a suppressant from the pharmacy?
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't add a cough syrup right now. Let's see what happens off the ramipril. Honey and water are fine if they soothe you, just don't expect them to fix it.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Fair. And if it doesn't settle, or if it gets worse before I see you?
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it gets worse, or you get breathless, a fever, or chest pain, call us or go to urgent care, don't sit on it. Otherwise I want you back here in four weeks to recheck the pressure and see about the cough.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks either way, even if the cough vanishes next Tuesday.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Even if it vanishes. The four-week visit is for the blood pressure on losartan, not only the cough.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. I over-explain, I know. The hardware store thing, the dog, the notebook, none of that changes the pill. I just don't like leaving stuff out.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): The timeline was the useful part. Anything else you wanted to ask while you're here?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Um. Will the losartan make me dizzy? The ramipril didn't, but new pills make me nervous. Also the pharmacy by the grocery closes at six and I parked in the short lot.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can make some people lightheaded, especially the first few doses. Stand up slowly, and if you feel faint, sit down and call us. Most people do fine.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Stand up slow, call if faint. I can do that. I'll start it tomorrow, not tonight, like you said.
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tomorrow morning is right. I'll see you in four weeks, Mr. Ellison.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, have a seat. What has been going on with you?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, Doctor. Thank you for fitting me in. I had a hernia operation ten days ago, and the wound has turned rather red.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Sorry to jump in. I'm his carer, I stay at the house during the week. The dressing was wet with a yellow stain this morning.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shame, that is not what you want after an operation. Tell me how the recovery had been going before this.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): The first several days were quite acceptable. I was moving about the house, slowly. Then the skin beside the cut began to look angry.
[SEG0006] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The sister next door took the plaster off just now, before we came in. She said there is yellow stuff on the gauze, and she left it open for you.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Helpful. Which side was the hernia, and did they do it open or with a camera?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): The right groin. It was an open repair, at the day theatre, and I went home the same afternoon. They put a mesh in, or so the surgeon told me.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did the redness start? As near as you can.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I am not entirely sure of the day. Perhaps Saturday, or it may have been Sunday. I cannot put a proper date on it.
[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I only saw the skin properly on Sunday evening, when I helped him shower. The dressing was still on before that.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did you feel feverish at all?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Last night, yes. I felt very hot, and shivery with it. I did not read the thermometer myself.
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Ja, I did. It was thirty-eight point nine... no, thirty-eight point four. I misread it the first glance, sorry.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right, thirty-eight point four last night. How are you feeling sitting here now?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Tired, Doctor, and rather washed out. The shivering has stopped. I still feel a little warm, but the fever seems to have settled.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the wound itself painful?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): It is. A burning pain, worse when I walk. If I sit, it eases.
[SEG0019] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He was awake a good part of the night with it. I did give him pain tablets, I'll explain in a moment.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): There was also the matter of the parking. The robot outside was out, and the boom was stuck, and we nearly turned around. I apologise for arriving a little flustered.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): No stress at all. Let me look at the wound. Just lie back a bit.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. The cut is in the right groin. The skin around it is red for about the length of my finger, and there is a little yellow discharge at the lower end. The stitches are still in. It feels warm. I am not feeling a pocket of pus underneath.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that a serious infection, Doctor?
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): I am not going to put a firm label on it this minute. It may be a superficial wound infection, it may be a stitch abscess, and I cannot rule out a small collection a bit deeper. I will not say the mesh is involved, not on today's look. We'll see what the tests say before I go further than that.
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The sister thought it looked infected, but she said you must decide.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. How is your appetite, and have you had any nausea or vomiting?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): My appetite has been poor since yesterday. I have not vomited. There has been no diarrhoea either.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): And passing urine? Any burning, or going more often?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): That has been entirely normal. No burning, and not more often.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any redness in the other groin, or red streaks down the thigh?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing of that sort.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He does get a bit short of breath on the stairs. He tells me that was already there before the operation, from not being fit.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll park the fitness for another visit. I don't want to chase that today. What medicine did they send you home with?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): An antibiotic, co-amoxiclav. The strength was five hundred... no, six hundred and twenty-five milligrams, three times a day, by mouth. They said it was to prevent infection after the operation.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): How many days did you actually take it?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Five days... or was it seven? I finished the packet. I honestly cannot tell you which it was.
[SEG0037] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The box is on the kitchen table at home. I think the label said a week, but I would not swear to that.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): And you are not taking it now?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Correct. I took the last tablet two or three days ago. I am not on it at present.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about pain relief?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Panado, the paracetamol, one gram by mouth, up to four times a day, when the pain requires it. Yesterday I also took ibuprofen, two hundred milligrams... forgive me, four hundred milligrams, by mouth, with food, twice.
[SEG0042] person_3 (CAREGIVER): While we are on tablets, his brother uses metformin for his diabetes. The brother was lecturing him about sugar on the phone. He has not taken any of his brother's tablets.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Quite so. My brother has diabetes. I do not. I did not take a single one of his tablets.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. We'll leave your brother's metformin right out of your notes. Are you on any regular medicine of your own? Blood pressure, anything like that?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. Nothing regular, apart from what I have already mentioned.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): How have you been looking after the wound at home?
[SEG0047] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We tried to keep it dry. He showered on Sunday and the dressing got damp, so I changed it with gauze from the chemist.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): I may also have walked too much. I went to the shops on Friday. Perhaps that provoked it.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Walking is usually encouraged after this operation, so I would not blame the shops. Let me take your numbers.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Temperature now is thirty-seven point six. Pulse is ninety-six. Blood pressure is one twenty-eight over seventy-eight. Your oxygen saturation is ninety-eight percent on room air.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Is a pulse of ninety-six a concern?
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): It is a little fast, which fits with your body dealing with this. Your tummy is soft, and there is no guarding away from the wound.
[SEG0053] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He only managed tea and one slice of toast this morning. I wasn't sure if I should mention that.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you did. Here is what I would like to do. I will take a wound swab now and send it to the lab. And I would rather change the antibiotic than restart the co-amoxiclav.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): What would you prefer I take, Doctor?
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Flucloxacillin, five hundred milligrams, by mouth, four times a day, for seven days, for this wound infection. Start this afternoon, if the pharmacy downstairs has stock.
[SEG0057] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And the old ones, should he... oh, he has already finished them. Sorry.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do not restart the co-amoxiclav. The flucloxacillin replaces it. Try to take it on an empty stomach, about an hour before food.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): I will be careful with the timing.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Carry on with the Panado as you have been, for the pain. For the ibuprofen, hold it. Actually, leave it off completely until I see you again. I don't want it on an empty stomach while we treat this.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Understood. I will stop the ibuprofen.
[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the redness spreads quickly, or the fever goes above thirty-eight point five again, or you start vomiting, go to casualty. Do not wait for me. Otherwise I want to see you here in two days.
[SEG0063] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Two days. I'll ask at the desk on the way out.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): And the stitches, Doctor? Should they come out?
[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): Leave them for now. If the swab, or the look of the wound when you return, suggests we should release a stitch, we can do that then. I am not opening it today.
[SEG0066] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The sister asked whether you want a dressing back on.
[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): A dry dressing is fine. Change it if it becomes soaked. Please don't pack anything into the wound.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): May I ask whether this is likely to spoil the repair?
[SEG0069] person_1 (DOCTOR): I do not think so, and I am not concluding that the repair has failed. Most wounds like this settle with antibiotics and simple care. I won't say more until the swab is back.
[SEG0070] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He was also fretting about work. He is a bookkeeper, mostly sitting at a desk.
[SEG0071] person_1 (DOCTOR): Desk work can start again when you feel up to it. No lifting anything heavier than a kettle until I review you. That is the bit I would stick to.
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. That is quite clear.
[SEG0073] person_1 (DOCTOR): The swab goes today, I will write the script, and reception can book the two-day visit. Anything you still want to ask?
[SEG0074] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. You have been most kind. We shall do exactly as you have said.
[SEG0075] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll watch that he takes the new antibiotic properly. Thank you.
[SEG0076] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pleasure. Look after that wound, and I will see you in two days.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Before we get into it, the parking was a mess, we circled twice, and I almost had Denise drop me at the curb.

[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, routine, though I've been turning the pills over in my head for weeks, Dr. Shah. I'm seventy-one in June, which is not why I came, I just keep announcing it.
[SEG0004] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I drove her. Frank, her husband, stayed home because his sugar's been up and down and he hates the waiting room.

[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Mostly okay, I think. I get tired, not sleepy-tired, more like the laundry basket feels heavier and I sit down in the middle of folding. I told myself it was just age, but it's been on my mind.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's been talking about being tired since before Christmas. I hear it most Mondays when I come in.

[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Would you say those cramps are worse since you changed your medicines, or about the same?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose... sometimes, not really. Some weeks yes, then I'll go ten days with nothing and think I imagined it. I wouldn't want you to write down that they got worse.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair, I won't hang a change on that. Any chest pain?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): No. None. I know that's the one you're supposed to speak up about, and I haven't had any.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Shortness of breath?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No. I can still get up the stairs, I just pause at the landing from the tired feeling, not because I can't breathe.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Dizziness, or lightheaded when you stand up?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No, not that. I stand up fine.
[SEG0019] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I haven't seen her grab for the wall or anything.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Tell me what you're actually taking. Start wherever you want.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): The blood pressure one I still take, for the high blood pressure I've had for years. Lisinopril, the little round one, ten milligrams. [SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm only there Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays. I set the lisinopril out those days, but she says she already took it, or that it's an off day, and I can't swear she's even doing every other day. Some weeks the bottle looks the same.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): I am mostly doing every other day. I think. The week the grandkids came I lost track, so I won't promise it's perfect.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ten milligrams, aimed at every other day, and neither of you is sure it actually happens that way. What about the cholesterol tablet?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): I stopped it. Atorvastatin, the one for my high cholesterol. I was going to say forty milligrams, that's what I started on years ago, but no, you cut it to twenty, twenty milligrams, and I stopped after I read something online.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did you stop?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Spring. I want to say March, after this long article, but it might have been later. I didn't write it down, I just put the bottle in the back of the cabinet.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It was still in the weekly box in April, I remember her birthday lunch, and then it wasn't. I can't give you a date either. Sometime in the spring.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): We don't need the exact day. What did you read?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): A health newsletter, then a Facebook thread, women my age saying statins ruined their muscles and their memory and their liver. [SEG0064] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll get her there tomorrow if they'll take her. Morning's free.

[SEG0081] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She'll ask me tomorrow if you ordered the A1c. I'll tell her no.

[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): What's the timeline, when did it begin?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Probably two weeks. Yeah.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ah.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): I've had poor appetite for two days too, for two days. There's being a bit constipated as well. With being a bit constipated, pretty severe, if I'm being honest.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, have you had a vague tummy ache before, or is this the first time?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit, last winter. It settled by itself back then.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll do your observations first.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sit still for a moment...
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay: BP is 108 over 80, temperature is 36.8 degrees. And respiratory rate 15, pulse is 81 beats a minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air.
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that alright, doctor?
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): They help me see the whole picture, more shortly.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Could you come over to the couch, please?
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm just checking this side.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your tummy is soft but tender low on the right with mild guarding, and the temperature is only a little up.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, you can get dressed. Let me check a few things. Any blood in the stool, vomiting or high fever?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I haven't had any of them.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had any urinary symptoms?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): I haven't noticed any urinary symptoms.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is your chest okay generally?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing there.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything with your nerves, like weakness or numbness?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about your medical history?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): I've got high blood pressure.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): I see, go ahead.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, anxiety.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, anxiety is known to us, good to have that clear. Are you taking anything regularly, including from the pharmacy?
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Escitalopram. I take it 10 milligrams, once a day for the anxiety.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is that long-standing?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): About nearly five years.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you active?
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): I walk the dog every morning.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Who lives with you?
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): My partner and our baby.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): How are your meals?
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): I grab fast food at lunch most days.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): What operations have you had, if any?
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I had a cataract operation in my left eye, about a year ago.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has anything ever caused you a reaction? I mean any allergies.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): No allergies at all.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): From what you've told me and what I found, the most likely explanation is possible appendicitis, which can look mild in older people.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm going to order blood tests, for abdominal pain. Let's get a CT scan of the abdomen, for right iliac fossa tenderness. Even though you look fairly well, I'd like the surgeons to see you today. I think the surgical team should see you too. If the symptoms get worse, that's the point to come in urgently.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Alright, I follow.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll catch up straight away. I think we're done unless you have questions.
[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor, goodbye.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Look after yourself.
