[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's a proper ache, deep in the knee. Worst going down the stairs. And it wakes me at night — I don't know, doctor, not every night, but a lot of them.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): So pain in the right knee, worse on the way down the stairs, and often at night. Have I got that straight?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): That's it. Going up isn't so bad. Down is horrible. I'm seventy-one and I feel about ninety on those stairs.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did it start?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Not last week. Maybe since around Christmas? Or was it the autumn? I can't put a date on it.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right, we won't force a date. Any swelling you've noticed, or the knee giving way under you?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling that I've seen. And it hasn't given way. It just hurts.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it lock, stick, and refuse to straighten?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any injury beforehand — a twist, a fall?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I didn't do anything to it. It just came on.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): What have you been putting on it, or taking for it?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I rub in the Voltarol. The gel. Most evenings — well, actually not every evening, but most — and sometimes in the morning if it's bad.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Diclofenac gel, on the right knee. And anything you swallow?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes those anti-inflammatory tablets from the chemist. Well, I say sometimes — maybe once or twice a week, I don't know, doctor. Just when I can't face the stairs.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): The nurse who booked you in has written diclofenac tablets, fifty milligrams. Is that what the box says?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifty? I thought the packet was twenty-five. Or maybe it is fifty. I don't know, doctor. I just take one tablet when it's bad.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the nursing note says fifty milligrams, you remember twenty-five, and it's one tablet now and then. I won't guess which box you've got at home.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Sorry. I should have brought them.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any stomach trouble with them? Indigestion, a bleed, anything of that sort?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No stomach problems at all.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): And apart from the knee, how are you in yourself? Any fever, or the knee hot and red?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. It's not red. I'm just tired of it, that's all.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tired of the pain, or a separate exhaustion, as if you're unwell?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): From the pain, I think. I don't know, doctor. I'm not ill.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave it as you mean it. Do you take anything else regular?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol, the odd two tablets, the five-hundred ones, if the gel isn't enough. And my water tablet in the morning, for the blood pressure.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): The water tablet — do you know the name? Bendroflumethiazide, perhaps?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. It's just the water tablet. Little white one. One each morning. Been on it for years.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, I'll record it as the water tablet until we see the box. You mentioned the blood pressure — that's still being treated?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, ongoing. The nurse checks it. I don't know the numbers.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Speaking of the nurse, she weighed you at ninety-one kilograms this morning.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Ninety-one? That can't be right. My bathroom scales said twelve stone four last Sunday. I don't know which to believe.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): So ninety-one kilos on our scale, twelve stone four at home. I won't average them. Has the weight been creeping up, do you think?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Maybe a bit. I don't know, doctor. I sit more these days, because of the knee.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): That fits with the knee. Before we go on — did you get here all right? The ring road was a nightmare when I came in.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, don't start me. I left at half eight and I was still crawling past the retail park at nine. Some lorry had shed a load of pallets.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pallets? On the dual carriageway?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Right across the inside lane. And the radio was on about the Test, and I nearly missed my turning because I was listening to the cricket.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Who's playing? I haven't seen a ball all week.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): England, somewhere hot. My grandson was texting me the score every five minutes. He's mad for it. Twelve years old and he knows every bowler's average.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dangerous knowledge at twelve. Does he play?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Club cricket on Saturdays, when it isn't raining. Last week he was more interested in the tea than the batting, mind you.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): The tea is half the point. Anyway — back to this knee, if I may.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, sorry, I do go on.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not at all. Let me think out loud for a moment, and I am not making a firm diagnosis. [SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): So you don't know either?
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not yet, and I'd rather say so. One thing from earlier — you said no stomach trouble. I just want to be sure about heartburn, acid, waking with a burn.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, I do get heartburn. At night, if I've eaten late. I didn't think of that as stomach trouble. It's been a few weeks, I suppose.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heartburn at night for a few weeks, especially after a late meal. That matters with those tablets. I'd rather you didn't take the diclofenac tablets for now.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): All right. The gel's fine, though?
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): The gel is reasonable to carry on with, on the knee, as you've been doing. And the paracetamol when you need it — up to two of the five-hundred milligram tablets, and not more than four times in a day.

[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Now, two things we could do, and I am not choosing today. Physiotherapy, to work on the stairs and the strength. Or a steroid injection into the knee. Either might help. Neither is booked.

[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then we leave both on the table. If the pain is no better in six weeks, come back and we'll pick one. If it settles, you needn't rush back.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. And if it gets worse before that?
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it swells up hard, goes hot, or you can't walk, don't wait the six weeks — ring us sooner. That's the safety net.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): I can do that.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit yourself down. What has you in today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this knee, doctor, the right one. Going down the stairs is a holy show, and then of a night it starts up on me again.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the stairs, in your own time.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): There's fourteen steps down to the hall, and the third from the bottom is the killer. I go down sideways, holding the rail like an old crab. Coming up isn't nearly as bad, which is odd.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has it been going on?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Five weeks. Well, no, I'm wrong — we had the communion early in the summer and I was grand then, so it's eight weeks. Definitely eight weeks.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): And what is it like at night?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I get to bed grand enough, and then around two, maybe half two, it aches deep in the joint. The pillow between the knees was a waste of money, it goes flat. I end up sitting on the edge of the bed until it eases.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it swell, or lock, or give way under you?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): It puffs up a small bit by the evening, over the kneecap. It doesn't lock, thank God. And it hasn't given way on me. I was worried after Josie next door went down in the supermarket, but that's her, not me.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any heat in the joint, or a fever with it?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. And it's not hot if I put my hand on it. Just sore, and a bit puffy, as I said.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Where exactly do you feel the pain?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): On the inside of the right knee, and under the kneecap on the way down the steps. If I sit too long at mass it stiffens up, and the first few steps after are desperate.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): What have you been doing for it yourself?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): The gel from the chemist, diclofenac, the one percent. I rub a finger's worth into the right knee twice a day — actually, no, it's three times a day, morning, after the dinner, and before bed.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any tablets along with the gel?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol by mouth, two of the five hundred milligram ones, most mornings. And now and again the diclofenac tablets, by mouth as well. I thought they were the twenty-five milligram, but I looked at the box this morning — they're fifty milligram.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often would you take the diclofenac tablet?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Not every day. Maybe two evenings in the week, if the stairs have been bad. I never swallow two of them together. My sister takes hers every day for her back, but I'm not doing that.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any stomach trouble from them at all?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No stomach problems at all. I was careful about that, because my mother had an ulcer from tablets years back, and I didn't want the same.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand. What else are you taking, prescribed or from the chemist?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): The blood pressure tablet, amlodipine, for the high blood pressure I've had for years. It was five milligrams for ages and then they put it up — no, sorry, it's ten milligrams now, by mouth, every morning.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): I do miss it the odd morning, if I'm rushing to the half eight mass. Not often. Most days it goes down me.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the plan is every morning, but you're not dead sure it happens every single day.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the truth of it, yes.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else sitting in the press?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Gaviscon. A spoonful by mouth when I need it, usually in the evening.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heartburn, is it?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, yes. I said no stomach problems and I meant no pain in the stomach itself, but I do get heartburn of an evening, the last few weeks. If I take the diclofenac tablet and lie down on the couch for the news, it burns up behind the breastbone. A spoon of Gaviscon settles it.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Can you put any date on when that heartburn started?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I couldn't tell you. It crept up on me. Not years, just lately, and I can't pin the day at all.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting, black stools, or food sticking on the way down?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): None of that. No vomiting, the bowels are grand, no black stools, and nothing sticking.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. No allergies that I know of.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Can I ask about your weight? It matters for a knee.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): I know, I know. I'm after putting on a bit since I stopped the bowling. Too many biscuits with the tea, if I'm honest, and no one in the house to give out to me.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): The note from the nurse this morning has you at ninety-one point five kilograms.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Those scales are miles out. I weighed myself at home yesterday, eighty-six — no, eighty-seven kilograms, in my socks, before the breakfast. I'd swear to the eighty-seven.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): So it's ninety-one point five on our note and eighty-seven on yours, and we won't settle which is right today.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Put the eighty-seven down as the true one. I still had the coat on for your one, I'd say. Theirs always reads high. Still and all, eighty-seven is what my own scales said.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll keep both figures. How are you managing around the house and out of it?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I live on my own since Paddy died, three years now. I was a primary teacher, retired ten years. I walk to mass most mornings, only about ten minutes and flat, though the hill home is another story. I gave up the bowling in the spring.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look at the knee now, if you're agreeable.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Fire ahead. It's the right one. The left never bothered me.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tender along the medial joint line of the right knee. There's a small effusion, nothing dramatic, and crepitus when I bend it. It straightens out fully, and there's no redness.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the exact spot, yes, when you press there. I got the same catch coming off the path outside the credit union last week.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Putting it together, this sounds like osteoarthritis of the right knee, wear and tear. I'm not calling it certain — it's my working impression from the story and from that examination.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother had the two knees done, so I was half waiting for it. She was eighty-two for the second one. I'm seventy-four in November, so I've a bit to go yet, please God.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did you ever have an operation yourself, on the knee or anywhere else?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Cataracts, the both eyes — the left one three years ago, and the right the year before that. Nothing ever on the knee. No scope, no surgery there at all.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): For this knee, two roads are worth a chat. Physiotherapy, to build the muscle above the knee, or a steroid injection into the joint. I don't want to decide that for you today.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Would the injection be done here in the treatment room? Josie had one and she was flying for months, though she also said the first week was worse, so I don't know which part to believe. And is the physio the place down on the Mall?
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Either one is reasonable. Physio if you'd rather avoid a needle, the injection if the night pain is what you want eased sooner. We might do one, we might do the other. Nothing is booked.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I think about it, so? I want to ask my daughter. She'll say I'm being dramatic, but she doesn't have my stairs.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): You think on it. Nothing goes ahead until you say the word.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): And if I picked the physio, how many times would I be trailing over there?
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Usually a short block of sessions, but we won't book it unless you want it. Same story for the injection — only if you decide you want it.

[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Since the hospital? Or before it? Honestly, I couldn't say. I've been off my food a while.

[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No, none of that. I'm just not hungry. ~

[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): It could be 30. The chemist knows. I only take what they give me.

[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): For my mood, after my wife died. Two years ago.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm very sorry. Any operations?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Gallbladder, in the nineties.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me weigh you, and check your numbers. ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Go on then. ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pulse 82, blood pressure 118 over 72, temperature 36.6, oxygen 96 percent, and you weigh 64 kilos.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that a lot? ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your record says 74 kilos a year ago, so you've lost about ten kilos, which is significant. Any cough or breathlessness left from the chest infection?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): A little cough in the morning. No breathlessness.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd say the main thing is poor appetite after your recent illness, in the setting of low mood, so I'd call it reduced appetite following illness.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Do you think it's my mood? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's likely part of it, but with that much weight loss, I don't want to assume. I'd like to arrange blood tests, to look for anaemia, thyroid, and other causes.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Meanwhile, small meals and snacks, six times a day, and a build-up drink between meals, rather than big plates.

[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's the idea. And try to eat with someone, if you can, a neighbour or a friend.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): My daughter comes on Sundays. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. I'd like to see you again in two weeks, and weigh you again.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Fine. Thank you, doctor. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in, sit. We've got a short slot, so what brings you in?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Months. Um, since last winter, or the one before, I couldn't tell you. It kind of snuck up.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Every day?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Most days. I crash around three. It's the job, and I'm fifty-two, so, you know.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): What do you do for work?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Office manager at a dental clinic. Phones, payroll, people calling out. My sister thinks I should get checked, she makes a federal case out of everything.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you feel cold when other people don't?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I live in a cardigan, even in July. Well, our AC is set to meat locker, so I wouldn't call it a real problem.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight up or down?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Up a little. Ten pounds, well, actually maybe fifteen. I don't own a scale, so don't write that in stone. It's the snacks at the front desk.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Same stretch of months?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I guess. Jeans got tight after the holidays and just stayed tight.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): How are your bowels?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): They're fine. Well, actually, I'm a bit backed up. Every two or three days instead of every morning. Hardly worth mentioning.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any straining or blood?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): A little straining. No blood. I don't take anything for it.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is your mood down?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I mean, I'm flat, kind of blah, but that's the schedule, not... I'm not depressed. I'm not crying in the car or anything.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hair thinning, dry skin, or a change in your voice?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no, and no. My husband would've mentioned the voice. He narrates my life.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): None of that. I can cross the parking lot just fine.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any thyroid disease in the family?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): My mom. She was on thyroid pills her whole adult life. Underactive, I think, or Graves. I always mix those two up.

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the water pill. The little white one, for my blood pressure. That's the only real medicine.

[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): HCTZ. Twenty-five milligrams, every morning. Been years. I don't miss doses, before you ask.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else? Pain pills, vitamins?

[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Drug allergies?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Nope. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thyroid isn't enlarged. No puffiness in the face. Pulse is seventy-six and regular. Pressure today is one thirty over eighty-six.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): See? Nothing dramatic. I almost canceled and went back to the desk.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working impression is an underactive thyroid. It might just be the hours and getting older. I can't call it yet.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll order a TSH and a free T4. Get the blood drawn this week, lab downstairs.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I have to? If it's borderline again they'll just shrug, and I'll have wasted a morning.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, you have to. Come back in two weeks and we'll go over the results. Keep taking the HCTZ, and don't start any thyroid pills off the internet.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Afternoon. Have a seat. What's the problem?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's my stomach, and I'm not sleeping, and I'm knackered the next day. They feed each other, really, the pain stops me sleeping and then I'm useless. I'm a bookkeeper, and I've been leaving the office early when it flares, which isn't like me.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Where is the pain?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Upper tummy, dead centre, just under the breastbone. It comes in bouts, especially late afternoon, a dull ache that sometimes burns, moderate rather than doubling-over. A big meal or coffee makes it worse, and a snack doesn't settle it. I wondered about my gallbladder, a colleague had hers out, but it's not off to the side.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I can't date it. Since Diwali or after, maybe. My neighbour had everyone round, there was so much food, and I remember pressing on my stomach in her kitchen, though it might have started before that.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Constant, or in bouts?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Bouts. It goes quiet, then it's back, especially late afternoon. I'm usually on the spreadsheets then, which is probably irrelevant, sorry.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Vomiting?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I feel a bit sick now and then, queasy, but I haven't actually been sick. No blood either, not that there's anything to bring up.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Black stools, or blood in the stool?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Once a day, brown, formed, nothing dramatic. Sorry, that's a lot of detail about something very ordinary.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lost any weight?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think so. My clothes fit the same, and I was about eleven stone at Christmas and I'm still there.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No temperature, and I haven't felt hot or shivery. I've still got a thermometer from covid in the drawer, unused, which says it all.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the sleep?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I drop off, then I'm awake around two or three, maybe four hours altogether. I was going to say weeks, well actually it's longer than the stomach, last winter or the one before, I can't date it. Sometimes the burning wakes me, other nights I'm awake first and then I notice the tummy. I lie there scrolling about ulcers, which is stupid, I know.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heartburn, acid coming up?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, if I lie flat. Two pillows help a bit, and if I slide down in the night it comes straight back. I've started sleeping almost sitting up, which plays havoc with my neck, but that's another story.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain? Breathless?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain, and I'm not breathless. My uncle had a heart attack in his fifties, so I did panic one evening, but it doesn't go into my arm.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Trouble swallowing?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No, food goes down fine. I had a scratchy throat for a week in the autumn, a cold, long gone, my nephew had the same thing.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ulcers or bowel cancer in the family?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Mum had a stomach ulcer years ago, on tablets for ages. No bowel cancer, not that anyone's mentioned.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. One cigarette at a party when I was sixteen, I coughed for an hour, and that was that.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alcohol?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Socially. An odd glass with friends, that sort of thing.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): How much in a week?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, if I'm straight about it, a bottle of wine most nights, perhaps. I open it while the pasta's on and it just goes. Socially was me making it sound better than it is.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Medicines, including from the chemist?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol, two tablets, when the ache is annoying, not every day. Ibuprofen as well when it's properly bad. My sister bought me vitamin D, but I don't really take that.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): What strength of ibuprofen, and how often?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): The four hundred milligram ones, just one. Maybe three times a week. I take it with a biscuit, which I suspect isn't how you're meant to.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none. Penicillin was fine when I had it for a tooth a few years ago.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Operations?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Appendix out when I was twenty-two. Only one. It might have been keyhole or a proper cut, I was too groggy to take it in, just a small scar on the right.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Diabetes? Blood pressure?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): No diabetes. Blood pressure's been fine at the chemist. I do get migraines, have done for years, though not in the last few months.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lie back. I'll examine your abdomen.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Soft. Tender in the epigastrium. No guarding, and no masses.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that's the exact spot, sorry I flinched. It's sore if I press it myself in the shower as well.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Could be acid, could be the ibuprofen irritating the lining, could be the wine. I'm not calling it an ulcer today, and I'm not saying it's your liver. Let's see what the tests say.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): So you're thinking it's just indigestion?
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Working impression is gastritis, and that's provisional. The poor sleep might be the pain or it might be the alcohol, and I won't split those today.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll start omeprazole, twenty milligrams, once every morning before breakfast, for four weeks. Stop the ibuprofen. Paracetamol is all right if you need something for the pain.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Will that clash with anything? I read it can thin your bones if you stay on it for years, and I got myself in a state about that at two in the morning.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Four weeks isn't years, and we'll look again when the bloods are back. No lecture on the wine. Cut it to a couple of glasses a week, not a bottle a night, and don't eat for three hours before bed.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bloods today, liver function, a full blood count, and a coeliac screen. Come back in two weeks for the results. If you vomit blood, pass black stool, or the pain turns severe, come back sooner.

[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): About three weeks, I'd say. Maybe a bit longer, but I only started really looking recently.

[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Most mornings, first thing. Less so later in the day. It's not every single time.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): I see. Anything else about the water itself? Colour, smell, how often you go?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): The colour's the usual straw sort of yellow. I go the normal amount, I think. Maybe once in the night.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right.

[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): How do you measure it?

[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, much more precise. The stick is a quick screen, and the lab test tells us what to make of it.

[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then we'd plan the next step together. I don't want to guess before we have the number.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Fair enough.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does anyone in the family have trouble with their kidneys?

[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): I see. That's useful for me to know.

[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell him to wait for the results too. We can talk about salt once we know more.

[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good to know. Let me just feel your tummy, if you'd lie back on the couch for me.

[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do ring the surgery if anything worries you. Otherwise, we'll contact you once the result is in.
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Lovely, thank you for explaining it so clearly. I feel better for having come.

[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have a good day.

[SEG0001] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, thank you. It's Rory, he's fifteen, he did his knee playing rugby six weeks ago, and he's still limping.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hello Rory. Which knee, and what happened?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): The left. I got tackled from the side, and my knee twisted, and I felt a pop.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Was there swelling, immediately?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. Within an hour. It was huge.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It was like a balloon. We took him to the emergency department, they said sprain, gave him a brace.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): How is it now?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): It's better, but it gives way on stairs, and it clicks, and I can't straighten it fully.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is there any locking, where it gets stuck?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Once or twice. It catches.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness, or any pain at night?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or redness on the knee?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): What have you been taking for the pain?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen, 200 mg, three times a day, with food.
[SEG0017] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, it's 400 mg, Rory. I gave him two tablets. And paracetamol, 500 mg, when he needs it.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll note that you and Mum gave different doses of ibuprofen, and I'll check which. Any other conditions?
[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He has mild asthma, hay fever, and eczema.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me check pulse and the rest. ~
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pulse 72, blood pressure 118 over 70, temperature 36.6, weight 62 kilos.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Fine? ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fine. Rory, lie down on the couch, and I'll examine the knee. Tell me when it hurts. ~
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's a little fluid in the left knee, and tenderness over the inner side of the joint line, and when I twist it, I get a click and pain. The ligaments feel stable.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): What does that mean? ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): It suggests a tear in the cartilage, the meniscus, rather than a ligament. Considering the twist and the locking, I'd say this is a probable meniscal tear.
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Will he need surgery? ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Possibly. I'd like to arrange an MRI scan of the left knee, to see exactly what's torn.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Can I play? ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): No rugby for now. Keep the knee moving, gentle exercises, and no twisting or running.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He won't like that. ~
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): No. ~
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): I know, Rory, and I'm sorry. But playing on a torn meniscus can make it worse. I'll refer you to the physio as well.
[SEG0036] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Okay. ~
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in three weeks, with the MRI result.
[SEG0038] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Three weeks. Thanks, doctor. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Mr Jacobs. Sleeve up for me, please, I'll do your observations before the doctor comes in.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, okay. Can we not drag it out? I've been in that waiting room since seven and I'm finished.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is one twenty-eight over seventy-eight, pulse eighty-eight, temperature thirty-six point eight. Oxygen sat is ninety-seven percent and you're breathing at eighteen a minute. Those are all fine on my side.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): They don't feel fine. This cough is doing my head in.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put the cough on the note. Your brother, when he dropped you off, mentioned a cousin who'd been ill, quite a long cough, and the family was worried it was TB. He wasn't sure it had been confirmed.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, please. My brother loves a story. I have not been near anyone with TB, and I haven't travelled anywhere. He can keep his opinions.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Howzit, Mr Jacobs, I'm Doctor Naidoo. Come, sit. Tell me what's been going on, in your own words.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the cough. Started with that flu and then it just stayed.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): The flu. How long has the cough actually been with you?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, about six weeks. Well, actually, the flu was six weeks ago, and the cough has been the whole six weeks. It maybe started a few days into the flu, and I can't give you the exact day.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): And through the day, how's it behaving?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Worse at night. I lie down and off it goes. Daytime it's there, but not so hectic, and I'm hardly sleeping, which is why I'm so ratty, sorry.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Don't apologise, shame. Was there fever, or was that only with the flu?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Fever was with the flu, and that's gone. The aches as well. I'm not hot now.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Are you bringing anything up, any phlegm?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. I can't honestly say.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll leave that one, then. Any blood?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about getting short of breath, or pain in the chest?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. I get a bit puffed on the stairs at work, but that's not new. The cough is what I came for.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): And your weight, any loss that you've noticed?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No weight loss.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Eating all right through all of this?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, I eat. Though, well, actually, my trousers are loose, I had to take the belt in two holes. They're hanging off me, and I didn't clock that as losing weight.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): That counts, thank you for saying it. Any drenching night sweats?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I wake up coughing, not sweating.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you been away recently, or around someone with tuberculosis?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I told Sister already. No travel. No TB contact. Work and home, that's my life.
[SEG0029] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry, Doctor, can I just come in. His brother was quite definite in the passage about a cousin in Polokwane, coughing for months, and the aunt thinks it was TB. Not confirmed, from what he said.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't buy that. I haven't seen that cousin in years, and my brother wasn't even there, he's just repeating my aunt's phone call. There was no contact.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. You don't recall any contact, and what reached me is second-hand and not confirmed. I'll note both, but I won't build a story on it.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Good. Can we get on with it? I've got a shift later, some bakkie has blocked the parking, and I'm already irritated.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll keep it moving. What do you do on that shift?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Warehouse, packing orders. It gets dusty. Nothing like the mines.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke at all?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Not hectic, about eight or ten a day. I keep saying I'll stop.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Are you taking anything for this cough, or any other medicine?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): A brown bottle from the chemist, some cough mixture. I take, um, two spoons at night, I think it's two. I never read the name on it.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): So we don't actually know the name, and the two spoons is a guess. Did anyone give you an antibiotic?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): The clinic did. Pink and white capsules, amoxicillin, five hundred milligrams, three times a day, for five days. I finished the lot about two weeks back, and the cough didn't care.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Finished, so that's stopped. Any regular tablets, for blood pressure or sugar or anything?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'm not a tablet person. Nothing else.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me listen to your chest. Big breath in, and out, and again. Your throat isn't red, the glands in your neck aren't up, and the chest is clear, no wheeze and no crackles.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): So it's nothing serious, then. Can I go?
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't call it nothing. Six weeks of cough, worse at night, and your clothes getting loose, that deserves a proper look. Folks will say post-viral cough, or a touch of asthma, or a lingering infection, or even TB, but I'm not naming a cause today, and I don't want to conclude any of those yet.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Then what am I supposed to do, just cough?
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): No. I'm sending you for a chest X-ray today, and the form goes in now. Let's see what the X-ray shows before anyone decides.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): And after that? I've got a shift, I can't keep coming back.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll book you back here next week to go through the result. Radiology is just down the passage, so you can do the film before you leave.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Next week. What if I get worse before that?
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): If your breathing gets tight, or you cough up any blood, or you feel properly unwell, don't wait for the appointment. Come back or go to casualty. Otherwise it's next week, and that visit is already booked.
[SEG0052] person_1 (NURSE): Come, I'll walk you as far as the passage. Radiology is the second door on the left.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Doctor, the tablets are not working. Still the room is spinning every time I turn in bed. I have not slept properly for days.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, let's go through it step by step. When you say spinning, the room moves around you, or you feel unsteady?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): The room moves, like a merry-go-round. It only lasts some seconds, maybe a minute, but it is so frightening. I hold the bed with both hands.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): That sounds unpleasant. And when did this first begin?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): About five weeks back. First I thought it was because of the heat, or low sugar, so I ate something and lay down, but it came again.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How often does it come now?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Every morning, when I turn on my side to get up. Sometimes also at night. Mostly when I turn to the right.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mostly to the right, interesting. Does anything else bring it on, apart from turning in bed?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Looking up at the shelf in the kitchen. Yesterday I looked up for the salt box and I had to catch the counter.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): And does anything make it settle, besides waiting?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Closing my eyes helps, and keeping still. That is all. Doctor, I saw a video on WhatsApp saying such things are from a brain tumour. Is it so?
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Those forwarded videos cause more worry than they ever cure. Nothing you've told me so far points to something dangerous, but let's carry on with my questions.
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, okay. Please ask.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting with the spinning?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No vomiting, only a little uneasy feeling in the stomach, and that passes.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any ringing in your ears?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no ringing. My hearing is the same as always, my husband still says I don't listen, ha ha.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha, that's a universal complaint. Now, you came to see the other doctor two weeks ago, and he started something. What are you taking?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Betahistine, 16 mg, three times a day. He said it is for the dizziness.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): And you've been taking it properly since then?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, morning, afternoon and night, with food. I have not missed one, I even set an alarm on my phone.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, that's useful for me to know. Are you taking anything else, any other tablets or supplements?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): No, only that one. Should I increase the dose? My neighbour says take double and it will work faster.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please don't double anything on a neighbour's advice. Stay on the dose you have for now. It can take a few weeks to show its full effect.

[SEG0002] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you, my dear. I'm afraid I've been rather foolish. I fell off a ladder, cleaning the gutters.
[SEG0003] person_3 (NURSE): Pulse 88, blood pressure 144 over 86, temperature 36.7.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good morning, Mr Hartley. I'm Dr Naylor. Tell me what happened. ~
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): I was about eight feet up, and the ladder slipped, and I came down on my left hand, with my arm out.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): When was that?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): About two hours ago. And my wrist has swollen up, rather alarmingly.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How bad is the pain?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Severe when I move it. I can hardly turn my hand over.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you hit your head, or hurt anywhere else?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no head injury. My right knee is a bit sore, but nothing much.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or tingling in your fingers?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): A little tingling in my thumb and index finger.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you have any medical problems?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): High blood pressure and an underactive thyroid.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): And do you do anything which might affect healing, do you smoke?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): I gave up thirty years ago.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look at your wrist. Tell me when it hurts.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Ow! There. ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): The wrist is swollen, with a visible bump, a deformity, on the back of it, it's very tender over the end of the radius, and the fingers are warm with a good pulse.
[SEG0021] person_3 (NURSE): His capillary refill is normal, doctor. ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, Chloe. Mr Hartley, this looks like a broken wrist, a fracture of the radius, called a Colles' fracture.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, bother. ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't be certain without an X-ray, and it could also involve a small bone in the wrist, so I'd like an X-ray of the wrist, and one of the knee.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Can I have something for the pain? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chloe will give you something strong right away. ~
[SEG0027] person_3 (NURSE): I'll bring it now. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please keep the arm raised on a pillow, and don't eat or drink anything until the X-rays are done, in case you need it set.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it need to be put back? ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Possibly. If the bone has shifted, we'll set it under local anaesthetic, in the department. ~
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): How very modern. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chloe will take you through to radiology. If your fingers go cold, blue or numb, tell her at once.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): I shall. Thank you. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on through, both of you. What would you like to sort out today?

[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He's been saying that since Monday. I thought we'd do the whole list while the pharmacy technician's still got his bag downstairs.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. Start wherever you like, what's the knee actually doing?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Right knee. Deep ache, and then a stab if I twist. Um, going round the shops sets it off something awful.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long's it been like that?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Six months. Well, actually, I was going to say since autumn, but six months sounds right. I think.
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Longer. He was limping at Christmas, so it's over a year. He just forgets.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't forget. I... Christmas is a blur. I'm saying six months.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): So we'll call it roughly six months to a year, and not pretend we've dated it. Is it there every day?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Most days. Mornings it's stiff, then it eases if I potter. Walking makes the ache worse. If I sit with the leg up it eases off a bit.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it swell, or give way under you?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Puffs up by the evening. Hasn't given way. I haven't fallen, touch wood.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the rest of you, chest pain, shortness of breath, trouble with the waterworks?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain, breathing's alright, waterworks are fine. I'm just sick of the knee.
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Sleep's a mess, though. He's up in the night with it.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): The knee wakes me, yes. I'm not depressed, if that's what you're thinking. I just can't get comfy.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): I wasn't thinking that. Before the tablets, did you get here alright? I was stuck on the bypass for ages.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Forty minutes, easy. A lorry had tipped pallets all over the retail park. Ridiculous.
[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Then this car park was full, so round the block we went. He had the cricket on the whole time.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): England were hopeless. My grandson Alfie had the radio on at breakfast, seven years old and shouting at the bowlers. I nearly switched it off.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And he made me pull in at the bakery. Cinnamon bun, icing on his jumper, doctor's waiting room. Honestly.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Worth it. Have you seen that sky? It's going to bucket down, my neighbour said. Her hanging baskets are already sulking.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): I left a sheet out on the line, so that'll be that. Shall we come back to the medicines? What are you taking just now?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): The pain ones, co-codamol. My water tablet. The sugar tablets for the diabetes. And the little white one for the cholesterol, atorvastatin, that's the name.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Take me through the co-codamol. What strength do you reckon, and how do you take it?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): The strong ones. Thirty with five hundred. Two tablets, four times a day. That's what goes down.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That's not what this says. The pharmacy technician printed the list off the bag. Co-codamol eight slash five hundred, two tablets up to four times a day.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Eight? That can't be mine. Are you reading the wrong line? The box looks exactly the same as last time.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then what you believe and what the list says don't match, and I'm not going to invent a strength. The two tablets, four times a day, you both happy with that bit?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Two, four times. I don't skip them. Why would the list be wrong? Could the technician have typed it wrong?
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Possibly. We'll let the chemist confirm it. Now, the water tablet, do you know what it actually is?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Bendro-thingy. Bendroflumethiazide. Two and a half milligrams, mornings. It's for the blood pressure. Makes me trot to the loo, mind.
[SEG0034] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He does take that every morning. I see him.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the sugar tablets, which ones, and how much?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Metformin. Five hundred milligrams twice a day, with my meals. Years I've been on those.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Atorvastatin next. What dose is on the packet?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Twenty milligrams at night. I think. Or forty? No, hang on, the packet says twenty. I'm fairly sure. Fairly.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's twenty. I looked on Sunday.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything you've come off, or a box you were given and never started?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Naproxen. I stopped that in March, it burned my stomach. And gabapentin, they handed me a box and I never took a single one. Still sitting there.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Gabapentin we simply ignore, then. Naproxen stays off. You said you wanted something stronger, what were you hoping for?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Tramadol. My neighbour gets it and she says it's marvellous. Or morphine, if that's what bad knees get. Why won't people just give it? Will it clash with the sugar tablets? What if I wake at three and I've already had four lots of co-codamol?
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not starting tramadol, and I'm not starting morphine. Let me think it through out loud. This could be the osteoarthritis grumbling, it could be extra time on your feet, it could be pain referred from the hip. I am not concluding any of those, and I am not calling it a nerve problem or a clot. Not from this chat.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): So you're saying you don't know? That's worse. What am I meant to do tonight?
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): I do have a working impression. It's your known osteoarthritis flaring in that right knee. That's the leading thought, and I'm stopping there.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Then a stronger tablet is obvious, isn't it? What about plain codeine? Or one of those gels? Is the gel useless? Will it count as another anti-inflammatory and burn me again?
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Plain codeine on top of co-codamol just stacks the codeine, so no. No tramadol either. A gel is different. I'll add ibuprofen gel, three times a day, rubbed on the knee. It's not the same as swallowing naproxen.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): And my stomach will be alright? I have a whisky on a Sunday, is that banned now? What about paracetamol from the corner shop as well?
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Gel on the skin is much kinder on the stomach; stop if the skin goes sore. Sunday whisky is fine. Don't add shop painkillers on top of the co-codamol.
[SEG0051] person_3 (CAREGIVER): One whisky, that's his lot. And he doesn't smoke, never has.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): May I have a look at the knee while you're here?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): If you must. It'll hurt, I'm warning you.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right knee's a little puffy, not red, and you flex to about ninety before you pull away. The hip moves freely, so that referral idea can sit down.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): See, it hurts. Are you sending me for an x-ray? What if it's cracked? Should I be on a stick?
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): No x-ray today. If it hasn't settled by the time I see you again, we might do a plain film, but I'm not booking it now. A stick only if you feel safer, not because I think it's broken.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): And you won't cancel the sugar tablets or the water one, will you? What if they send the weak co-codamol and it's not enough? Can I take an extra two?
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll re-authorise the metformin, the bendroflumethiazide and the atorvastatin exactly as they are. Co-codamol stays, but I will not increase it, and the chemist confirms eight or thirty before the next issue. No extra tablets. I'll add the ibuprofen gel to the repeat.
[SEG0059] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll phone the chemist after this and make them read the bag back to me.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Come back and see me in six weeks either way. Sooner if the knee blows up, you can't walk on it, or it goes hot and red.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks is ages. What if the gel runs out? Should I keep pottering in the garden or will I ruin it? And ice, is ice daft?
[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep pottering, little and often, leg up when it throbs, ice in a tea towel for ten minutes if it's puffy. The gel's on the repeat so it shouldn't run out. Any allergies before I send the script?
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. I've had penicillin, no rash, no trouble. I'm not allergic to anything.
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then we're done. Go careful if that rain starts.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr Hale, in you come. I took your blood pressure in the corridor because you looked flushed, and it was up, so Dr Okonkwo should see the figures as well as your form.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Flushed, yes, well the corridor's boiling and I'd legged it from the car park, Pauline had the meter running, and the card machine rejected me twice, so I was all wound up, which is a silly way to arrive when all I actually need is this occupational health form for work.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, Mr Hale, I'm Dr Okonkwo. Sit yourself down. What's brought you in today, in your own words?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): So I work in the council housing office, a desk job, and I mentioned to my manager that my right knee aches, which I now think was a mistake, because they've stopped me doing the stair inspections until a doctor signs this form to say I'm alright for the desk work, even though I sit down nearly all day.
[SEG0005] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'm Pauline, I drive him Tuesdays and Fridays. The form's in the blue folder, and he will talk the hind leg off a donkey if you let him.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's quite alright, Pauline, the detail helps. Nurse, what did you get for the blood pressure?
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): First reading, once he was sat, was one hundred and seventy-two over ninety-eight.
[SEG0008] person_1 (NURSE): I left it a couple of minutes and did it again. The second was one hundred and sixty-four over ninety-two, and his pulse was seventy-six and regular.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): That is the white coat business, I'm sure of it. It does this every single time I come in, and then I go home and I'm fine, and I feel completely well. If you feel well you assume the machine in the clinic is just being dramatic.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): White coat is ever so common, so I won't jump. How has the knee been for you?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): It's an ache, right knee, across the front, not a stabbing pain. Stairs in the multi-storey make it worse, sitting eases it, and I wouldn't say it's severe, more a nuisance that clicks into my head when I'm walking back from the photocopier.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): And how long has the ache been there?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I can't put a date on it, I'm afraid. Sometime after the clocks went back, or it might have been before, last autumn or the winter, and I genuinely could not tell you which.
[SEG0014] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He was limping a bit at Christmas, when I took him for the turkey. I only see him two days a week, so I miss bits.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Christmas rings a bell, though I was also hauling boxes of files that week, so the limp might have been that. Either way I still can't tell you when it actually started.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does the knee lock, or give way under you?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No, it doesn't lock, and it has never given way. I'm steady on my feet. Pauline's very strict about that.
[SEG0018] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He is steady. I wouldn't have him driving if he wasn't.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. With those blood pressure numbers, any headache, chest pain, or breathlessness?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No headache, no chest pain, and I'm not breathless. I feel well in myself, which is exactly why I think this is white coat and not some silent disaster, though I do know people say high blood pressure doesn't announce itself.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): My dad had a stroke, incidentally, years back, in his seventies. I only say it because it popped into my head, not because I'm building a case. He lived on a good while after.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thank you, that's useful to know, even in passing. What do you make of these clinic readings yourself?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): I make them out to be nerves. They did a cholesterol at a health check once, and the nurse then said it was borderline, but she never gave me a figure I can remember, and nobody started me on a tablet.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you remember when that cholesterol check was?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. A good few years ago, could be five, could be more, and I haven't a clue about the month.
[SEG0026] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He still buys the full-fat cheese, whatever he says about easing off. Sorry, Graham.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): I did try to ease off, Pauline, for about a fortnight, and then Christmas happened. Anyway, that's not why we're here.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. Given the clinic readings, and your dad's stroke sitting in the background, I think I'd like to start a small dose of amlodipine today, five milligrams.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. A tablet, today. I wasn't expecting that, if I'm honest, because I feel fine and the form is the thing I came for, and a new tablet might make me woozy at the office, which would be a whole other form.
[SEG0030] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Before you write it, doctor, he's got a monitor at home. He doesn't use it like he should, mind.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Go on, what sort of figures does he get at home?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I used it on Sunday. I thought it said one hundred and thirty over eighty, but no, hang on, I've got the scrap in my wallet, it was one hundred and twenty-two over seventy-eight.
[SEG0033] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And he was gabbling and sweaty in your waiting room, same as always. The second clinic one had already come down a bit, hadn't it, nurse?
[SEG0034] person_1 (NURSE): It had. One hundred and sixty-four over ninety-two from one hundred and seventy-two over ninety-eight. Still high, but it was falling while he sat.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I also had a large coffee in the car, which I shouldn't have, and I'd rushed, as I said, so I don't think today is a fair day to judge my blood pressure for the rest of my life and stick me on a tablet forever.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's new information, and it does change things. I suspect white coat hypertension, though I can't be sure from today, so you've talked me out of starting amlodipine.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): We won't start any blood pressure tablets today. I'd rather you check it at home, morning and evening, seated, for a week, and bring the readings in.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I can do that. The monitor's the Omron one from Boots, Pauline set the date on it because I got the year wrong, which is typical, and I'll write them in the notebook if I remember. I might forget the evening one if Match of the Day is on.
[SEG0039] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll remind him on Tuesdays and Fridays. The other evenings he's on his own, so I can't promise those.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's plenty. Use the same arm, sitting quietly for a few minutes first, and don't bother if you've just dashed up the stairs.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Right arm, I assume, that's the one they always use. And what about the knee form, because my manager will be on at me, and Friday is when they wanted it, though Monday would do if the post is slow, which it is round our way.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me look at the knee before I sign anything. Hop on the couch, or just swing round in the chair, whichever is easier.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Chair is easier. The couch is a bit high and I'd make a meal of getting down, and then we'd be here all afternoon, and Pauline's got another client at half twelve.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): No swelling that I can see, and it's not hot. You bend it fully, and it's a bit tender over the front if I press. Nothing worrying there.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Tender, yes, that's the spot, just under the kneecap. It's only the right, the left has always been fine, touch wood, even after that fun run I did and regretted.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): So this is a straightforward ache at the front of the right knee. I don't think you need a scan for it.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Good, because I hate those machines. My brother had an MRI for his back and he said it was like being posted through a letterbox, and I've got broad shoulders.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll sign the occupational health form to say you're fit for your desk job. I'd lay off lots of stairs for a couple of weeks while it settles.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol helps the knee a bit. I take two of the five-hundred milligram ones, so a gram, not every day, just when I've been on the stairs.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's a sensible dose. Carry on with that as you need it. No anti-inflammatory if you can help it, with the blood pressure question still open.
[SEG0051] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He had ibuprofen in the cupboard from his brother. I told him not to take his brother's tablets.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't take them. I just looked at the box. His name's on it, Derek, which is not me.
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. Stick to your own paracetamol. Now, for the pressure, a week of home readings, then I want to see you back here with the notebook.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): In a week exactly, or roughly a week? Only I've got a half day Thursday week, and parking is easier then, and if the readings are all normal I don't want to be started on a tablet at that visit either.
[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): Book about a week from today, Thursday is fine if that's when you can park. If the home readings are truly normal we still won't start tablets. We'll decide when we see them.
[SEG0056] person_1 (NURSE): I can book that at the desk on your way out, Mr Hale. And I'll print a little home blood pressure sheet if you want lines to write on.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes please, lines are better, my handwriting goes walkabout. And can you put morning and evening on it so Pauline can tell me off properly.
[SEG0058] person_3 (DOCTOR): Nurse Bennett will sort the sheet and the appointment. Anything else worrying you, even if it feels minor?
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Not medically. The meter in the car park ate my change once last month, but that's the council, and I work for them, so I shouldn't complain, except I will, at the water cooler, at length.
[SEG0060] person_4 (CAREGIVER): We'll be off, then. I'll make sure the notebook actually comes back with him.
[SEG0061] person_3 (DOCTOR): Lovely. No new tablets today, home readings for a week, and the form will be signed before you leave. Take care, both of you.

[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm a taxi driver. Windows down in summer, a lot.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pulse and temperature, please. ~

[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in four weeks. If it turns red, painful, or swollen at the corner, come back sooner.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Four weeks. Thank you, doctor. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. Come through and take a seat. The highway looked nasty — was the traffic bad on your way in?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): That is correct. I would be grateful if we could review the regular medicines and, if you thought it appropriate, something a little stronger for the knees.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. In your own words, how are the knees behaving?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Both of them ache, the right more than the left. It is a dull pain, moderate I would say, and it has been present for five-ish years. Stairs and the walk to the shops are the worst of it.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Five-ish years, both knees. What takes the edge off, if anything?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Rest helps, and the paracetamol does take the edge off, though it never truly settles, particularly in the evenings. I take paracetamol five hundred milligrams, two tablets, four times a day.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the anti-inflammatory — still on that?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Meloxicam, fifteen milligrams, once each morning with breakfast. I have been on it for about two years, for the osteoarthritis.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any heartburn with it, or black stools?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No heartburn, and no black stools. I am quite careful to take it with food.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. The pharmacy technician printed the chemist list this morning, so I'll read it and you tell me if it matches. Atorvastatin twenty milligrams at night, ramipril five milligrams in the morning, plus the paracetamol and the meloxicam as you've just said.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): The ramipril five milligrams each morning is correct. The atorvastatin, however, is not — I take forty milligrams at night. Well, actually, the packet at home plainly says forty. My previous doctor increased it, though I cannot recall the month.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hmm. Twenty on the pharmacy list, forty on your packet. I'm not going to pick a winner without seeing the box, so the dose stays unsettled for today.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I do apologise for the confusion. I also, um, miss the occasional night with it, if I am being honest. Perhaps two nights a week.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's worth knowing, and it muddies things further. Bring the box next time and we'll reconcile it properly. I won't issue a statin script today.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Of course. I shall bring it.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Now, the stronger painkiller. You were hoping for something more than the paracetamol and the meloxicam.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. I wondered whether tramadol might be suitable. A friend mentioned oxycodone, but I would not wish to be presumptuous. I simply find the evenings difficult.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me think this through out loud. Full-dose paracetamol, daily meloxicam, longstanding osteoarthritis. I could start tramadol fifty milligrams twice a day — sorry, no, fifty milligrams at night to start, not twice. That was my first thought.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): If you felt that was suitable, I would be most grateful.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Before I commit to that, any dizziness? Any falls?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): There was one turn of dizziness last month. I nearly fell in the kitchen. It passed within a few minutes, and it has not come back.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ah, that changes it. Tramadol, or oxycodone for that matter, would be a poor idea after a near-fall, especially with the ramipril on board. I'm not prescribing either. Scratch the tramadol.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand completely. I would rather be safe.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): I had also been going to order a kidney blood test today, what with the meloxicam and the ramipril together.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I had blood tests at the public hospital about three weeks ago. They told me the kidneys were all right. The letter is at home with the statin box.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then I won't order bloods today. If that letter doesn't actually show a kidney result, we'll do the test when you come back. No point sticking you twice.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): That seems very sensible. Thank you.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): While I write the other scripts — paracetamol, meloxicam and the ramipril, same doses you've confirmed — how was the rest of the drive, apart from the servo?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, the highway was crawling. A cricket match was letting out at the oval, the under-fourteens, and the cars were banked up for ages.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is your grandson still in that side?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, young Thomas. He bowled four overs on Saturday and was terribly pleased with himself. They lost, mind you, but he took a wicket with a slower ball, or so he tells me.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): A slower ball at that age, good on him. The weather held for you, at least. It bucketed down here on Friday arvo.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): We were lucky. His mother packed oranges and he ate the lot. He has asked for new white boots for his birthday, which I fear will be filthy within a week.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): They always are. Right — back to the scripts, before I lose my place.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): There is one other thing, if I may. There is a little morning stiffness, perhaps ten minutes, and then it loosens.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ten minutes is more the wear-and-tear pattern than an inflammatory one. I think this is osteoarthritis of the knees, the same diagnosis you've carried. I'm not calling it anything new.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that is what I was told. I have no swelling that I can see, if that is of any relevance. I do apologise for not mentioning the stiffness earlier.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): No harm done. Let me just feel the right knee. No warmth, and no fluid in the joint. There is crepitus when you bend it, and the left one is quieter.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): It does click, yes. Is there anything I ought to do differently at home?
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep the paracetamol regular, not only when the pain is bad — two tablets, four times a day, as you are already doing. Do not add ibuprofen, or any other anti-inflammatory, on top of the meloxicam. A warm pack in the evening is perfectly reasonable.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall do that. I do not take ibuprofen.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in four weeks with the statin box and the hospital letter. If the pain becomes severe before then, come back sooner and we'll rethink, still without jumping to an opioid.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate you explaining it so carefully, and I shall see you in four weeks.

[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): How much trouble does it give you?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I'd say mild. As for feeling exhausted, I honestly can't say when that began. It might have been last month or the month before.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): How much does it limit you?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I'd call it mild. And a fever, too. With fever, I'd say mild. I'd say all the time.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is there anything relevant on the family side?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother had a stroke.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you react to any medicines or foods? Any allergies?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think I have any, uh, no.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Can you list what you take, tablets, creams or inhalers?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm on rosuvastatin, 10 milligrams, at night. Though honestly, some days I forget to take it. Metoprolol. I take it 50 milligrams, twice a day for my pressure. Throat lozenges. I take it when needed.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ah. Tell me about any past illnesses or ongoing conditions.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): High cholesterol, for about a year. My family kept telling me to get it checked.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ah.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I have high blood pressure, for two years.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, high blood pressure is known to us, good to have that clear. Is there someone at home?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): My husband and I live above the shop.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you in work at the moment?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, I work in a bakery, early starts.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, anything you do to stay fit?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I do a yoga class on Thursdays.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything surgical in your history?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I had part of my thyroid removed years back.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): A few quick ones: jaundice, rash or difficulty breathing?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no jaundice, rash or difficulty breathing.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has there been any tummy pain on the left?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Definitely no tummy pain on the left.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm-hmm. Any breathing difficulties apart from this?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No problems with breathing.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Can I check a few measurements before we carry on?
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep your arm relaxed for me...
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay: heart rate 90, saturation 95 percent, temperature 38.2, pressure 120 over 73.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that normal?
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll come back to the numbers.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, let's have a proper look at you.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Raise your arm for me.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your tonsils are large with white coating and the glands in the neck are tender.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Please sit back down.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): From what you've told me and what I found, this looks most like glandular fever. I want to be honest that this is an impression, not a final answer. I can't rule out streptococcal tonsillitis yet.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, I'm scared it's something bad. Is it?
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's reasonable to be concerned, but right now glandular fever is my leading thought, not anything worse. Let me repeat that back to make sure. You've had swollen glands in your neck, since Friday, mild, and no rash or jaundice.

[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm going to order a monospot test, for sore throat and fatigue. Rest, plenty of fluids, and no contact sport for a month because of the spleen. Please come and see me in two weeks. Anything else on your mind before you go?
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Good, thanks, I'll see you then.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Goodbye for now.
